chunks.title: Module 09 — Trading Systems & Quant: From Idea to Evidence > 6. Metrics
chunks.text:
Module 09 — Trading Systems & Quant: From Idea to Evidence > 6. Metrics
6. Metrics

```
CAGR = (End/Start)^(1/years) − 1
Sharpe = mean excess/σ × √252
Sortino = mean excess/downside σ × √252
Calmar = CAGR/Max DD
Max DD = worst peak-to-trough
Profit factor = gross profit/gross loss
Expectancy = win%×avg win − loss%×avg loss
Win rate, payoff ratio, exposure, turnover, capacity
```

**Good retail range after costs:** CAGR 15–25%, max DD <20%, Sharpe >1, PF >1.3,
expectancy >0.2R, 100+ trades, multiple regimes, OOS positive.

High Sharpe on 20 trades = noise. Smooth equity can hide tail risk.

---

chunks.title: Module 09 — Trading Systems & Quant: From Idea to Evidence > 7. Robustness
chunks.text:
Module 09 — Trading Systems & Quant: From Idea to Evidence > 7. Robustness
7. Robustness

- **Walk-forward:** rolling in-sample/out-of-sample; report OOS only.
- **Out-of-sample:** hold out recent 20–30% or another market/regime.
- **Parameter sensitivity:** plateau, not a sharp peak.
- **Monte Carlo:** distribution of CAGR/DD/ruin.
- **Regime analysis:** trend/range, high/low vol, bull/bear.
- **Cost sensitivity:** double costs; edge should survive.
- **Multiple testing:** deflated Sharpe, White's Reality Check, PBO.

---

chunks.title: Module 09 — Trading Systems & Quant: From Idea to Evidence > 8. Deflated Sharpe / overfitting
chunks.text:
Module 09 — Trading Systems & Quant: From Idea to Evidence > 8. Deflated Sharpe / overfitting
8. Deflated Sharpe / overfitting

The more variants you test, the higher the expected max Sharpe by luck. Deflated
Sharpe adjusts for number of trials, skew, kurtosis and sample length. If you tested
50 variants, demand much more than Sharpe 1.0.

**PBO:** probability that the best in-sample strategy underperforms the median OOS.
Prefer low PBO.

chunks.title: Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin
chunks.text:
Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin
Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin

**Level:** Advanced · **Time:** 8 hours · **Prerequisite:** Modules 05, 07

> Trading builds returns. Portfolio construction **keeps** them. The goal is not the
> highest return in a good year; it is the best **risk-adjusted, survivable** return
> over decades.

---

chunks.title: Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > Learning outcomes
chunks.text:
Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > Learning outcomes
Learning outcomes

1. Build an asset allocation matched to goals and risk capacity.
2. Understand diversification, correlation and the efficient frontier.
3. Use factor investing (momentum, value, quality, low vol).
4. Rebalance systematically and control drawdowns.
5. Separate trading capital from long-term wealth.

---

chunks.title: Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 1. Asset allocation
chunks.text:
Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 1. Asset allocation
1. Asset allocation

| Asset | Role | Risk | Liquidity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equity | Growth | High | High |
| Debt/G-secs | Stability, income | Low–medium | High |
| Gold | Inflation/hedge | Medium | High |
| Real estate/REITs | Income, inflation | Medium | Low–high |
| Cash/liquid funds | Optionality, emergencies | Very low | High |

**Rule of thumb:** equity allocation ≈ 100 − age (aggressive), but adjust for:
- income stability,
- emergency fund,
- debt,
- time horizon,
- drawdown tolerance,
- dependents.

**Emergency fund:** 6–12 months expenses, separate from trading capital.

---

chunks.title: Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 2. Modern portfolio theory (in practice)
chunks.text:
Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 2. Modern portfolio theory (in practice)
2. Modern portfolio theory (in practice)

```
Expected portfolio return = Σ w_i×E(R_i)
Portfolio variance = ΣΣ w_i w_j σ_i σ_j ρ_ij
Sharpe = (E(Rp) − Rf)/σp
```

Diversification works when correlations <1. In a crisis, correlations converge — so
also diversify across **factors, geographies and asset classes**, not just stocks.

**Efficient frontier:** maximum return for a given risk. In practice, inputs are noisy;
use robust allocations, not optimised corner solutions.

---

chunks.title: Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 3. Factor investing
chunks.text:
Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 3. Factor investing
3. Factor investing

| Factor | What | India proxy | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Momentum | Winners keep winning | Nifty 200 Momentum 30 | Crash/reversal |
| Value | Cheap fundamentals | Nifty 50 Value 20 | Value trap |
| Quality | High ROE, low debt | Nifty 100 Quality 30 | Expensive |
| Low volatility | Stable returns | Nifty Low Vol 20 | Underperform in bull |
| Size | Small caps premium | Nifty Smallcap 250 | Liquidity/vol |
| Dividend | Income | Nifty Dividend Opportunities | Payout risk |

**Factor portfolio:** combine 2–4 factors, rebalance semi-annually, watch valuation
spreads. Factors can underperform for years — that is the premium.

chunks.title: Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 4. Core–satellite structure
chunks.text:
Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 4. Core–satellite structure
4. Core–satellite structure

```
Core (70–85%): index funds/ETFs, large-cap, debt, gold
Satellite (15–30%): active stocks, sector bets, trading
```

- Core = low cost, diversified, long-term.
- Satellite = concentrated, high-conviction, risk-managed.
- **Trading capital** should be a separate bucket with a hard limit (e.g., 10–20% of
  liquid net worth), never borrowed.

---

chunks.title: Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 5. Rebalancing
chunks.text:
Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 5. Rebalancing
5. Rebalancing

**Calendar:** quarterly/semi-annual.
**Threshold:** when an asset drifts >5% from target.
**Tax-aware:** use new inflows, dividends, and tax-loss harvesting; avoid unnecessary
STCG.

Rebalancing forces **buy low, sell high** and controls risk drift.

---

chunks.title: Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 6. Mutual funds and ETFs
chunks.text:
Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 6. Mutual funds and ETFs
6. Mutual funds and ETFs

| | Active MF | Index MF | ETF |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost | Higher | Low | Lowest |
| Tracking error | N/A | Low | Very low |
| Liquidity | NAV | NAV | Exchange |
| Best for | Skill-dependent | Core | Core/intraday |

**Selection:** expense ratio, tracking error, AUM, liquidity, fund manager tenure,
overlap, tax efficiency.

**SIP:** rupee-cost averaging reduces timing risk; market risk remains.
**Step-up SIP:** increase with income.

---

chunks.title: Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 7. Goal planning
chunks.text:
Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 7. Goal planning
7. Goal planning

```
Future value = P × (1+r)^n + SIP × [((1+r)^n − 1)/r]
```

Example: ₹10,000/month for 20 years at 12% → ~₹99 lakh (pre-tax). Use real returns
(after inflation) for goal setting.

**Goals:** emergency, insurance, home, education, retirement. Map each to a horizon
and asset mix. Do not use trading capital for short-term goals.

---

chunks.title: Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 8. Drawdown and withdrawal
chunks.text:
Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 8. Drawdown and withdrawal
8. Drawdown and withdrawal

- **Accumulation:** volatility is tolerable if horizon is long.
- **Retirement/withdrawal:** sequence-of-returns risk — early losses hurt more.
- **Bucket strategy:** 1–2 years cash, 3–5 years debt, rest equity.
- **Safe withdrawal:** 3–4% rule as a starting point; adjust for India inflation/taxes.

---

chunks.title: Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 9. Insurance and risk transfer
chunks.text:
Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 9. Insurance and risk transfer
9. Insurance and risk transfer

- **Term life:** 10–15× annual income, until dependents are independent.
- **Health:** family floater + super top-up.
- **Disability:** income protection.
- **Avoid:** investment-linked insurance with high costs/opaque returns.

Insurance is for **catastrophic risk**, not returns.

---

chunks.title: Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 10. Behaviour and wealth
chunks.text:
Module 10 — Portfolio & Wealth: Compounding Without Ruin > 10. Behaviour and wealth
10. Behaviour and wealth

- Automate investments; remove monthly discretion.
- Don't check the portfolio daily.
- Keep trading and investing in separate accounts.
- Rebalance mechanically.
- Avoid lifestyle inflation.
- Track net worth, not just returns.
- The biggest risk is usually the investor, not the market.

chunks.title: Module 11 — Taxation & Compliance for Indian Traders > 3. Capital gains computation
chunks.text:
Module 11 — Taxation & Compliance for Indian Traders > 3. Capital gains computation
3. Capital gains computation

```
LTCG/STCG = Sale consideration − Cost of acquisition − Transfer expenses
```

- Use **FIFO** for shares unless specific identification is allowed.
- Bonus/split adjust cost and quantity.
- Grandfathered acquisitions (pre-2018 equity) may have a higher cost basis — verify.
- Set-off: capital losses can offset capital gains; speculative losses only against
  speculative gains; F&O business losses against business income (rules apply).
- Carry forward: up to 8 years if ITR filed on time.

**Example:**
Buy 100 shares at ₹500 = ₹50,000; sell at ₹700 = ₹70,000 after 18 months.
LTCG = ₹20,000; exemption ₹1.25L → tax ₹0 (if no other LTCG). If LTCG = ₹2,00,000 →
taxable ₹75,000 × 12.5% = ₹9,375 + cess.

---

chunks.title: Module 11 — Taxation & Compliance for Indian Traders > 4. F&O taxation
chunks.text:
Module 11 — Taxation & Compliance for Indian Traders > 4. F&O taxation
4. F&O taxation

- F&O is **non-speculative business income**.
- **Turnover (ICAI guidance):** sum of absolute profits + absolute losses + premium
  received on sale of options (current guidance). Some practitioners include
  settlement value.
- Expenses deductible: brokerage, STT (as business expense for F&O), internet, data,
  advisory, depreciation on equipment (apportioned).
- **Audit:** under Section 44AB, turnover threshold (₹1 crore, higher with digital
  payments) and the 44AD/44ADA conditions matter. F&O often triggers audit if income
  is below the presumptive threshold and turnover is above the basic limit. Verify.
- **Presumptive:** Section 44AD (6%/8% deemed profit) may be available for eligible
  businesses; F&O eligibility is debated.
- **Advance tax:** quarterly (15%, 45%, 75%, 100%) if liability > ₹10,000.
- **ITR-3** for F&O business; **ITR-2** for capital gains only; **ITR-4** for
  presumptive business.

chunks.title: Module 11 — Taxation & Compliance for Indian Traders > 6. SEBI compliance for traders
chunks.text:
Module 11 — Taxation & Compliance for Indian Traders > 6. SEBI compliance for traders
6. SEBI compliance for traders

- **KYC** up to date; PAN-Aadhaar linkage.
- **Broker** must be SEBI-registered.
- **Algo trading:** broker approval, exchange registration, unique ID.
- **Insider trading:** don't trade on unpublished price-sensitive information.
- **Market manipulation:** no circular trading, spoofing, pump-and-dump.
- **Advisory:** giving advice for fee requires SEBI registration (RA/IA).
- **Records:** maintain order/trade logs for the required period.

**Penalties can exceed profits.** Compliance is not optional.

---

chunks.title: Module 11 — Taxation & Compliance for Indian Traders > 7. Tax-aware trading
chunks.text:
Module 11 — Taxation & Compliance for Indian Traders > 7. Tax-aware trading
7. Tax-aware trading

1. Prefer LTCG where horizon permits (12+ months).
2. Harvest losses to offset gains (within rules).
3. Avoid unnecessary churn in delivery equity.
4. Consider tax impact in strategy selection (intraday vs positional).
5. Keep a separate bank account for trading; simplify reconciliation.
6. Don't let tax drive a bad investment — but don't ignore it either.

```
Strategy:
Period:
Trades:
CAGR:
Sharpe:
Sortino:
Calmar:
Max DD:
Profit factor:
Expectancy (R):
Win rate:
Avg win/loss:
Exposure:
OOS CAGR/DD:
Monte Carlo 5th percentile:
Cost sensitivity:
Failure modes:
Verdict:
```

**Reject if:** <100 trades, no OOS, edge disappears with 2× costs, max DD > tolerance,

chunks.text:
Module 12 — Capstone: Build Your Complete Trading System > Phase 4 — Paper trading (90 days)
Phase 4 — Paper trading (90 days)

Rules:
- Same capital size as planned (mental accounting).
- Same order types and timing.
- Journal every trade daily.
- No rule changes mid-quarter unless a safety issue.
- Weekly review; monthly audit.

Track:
```
Trades, win rate, expectancy, PF, max DD
Plan adherence %, mistake counts
Slippage vs backtest
Live vs backtest divergence
Emotional events/tilt
```

**Pass criteria:** positive expectancy after costs, plan adherence >80%, max DD within
policy, no risk-limit breach.

---

chunks.title: Module 12 — Capstone: Build Your Complete Trading System > Phase 5 — Review and scale
chunks.text:
Module 12 — Capstone: Build Your Complete Trading System > Phase 5 — Review and scale
Phase 5 — Review and scale

```
1. Compare live vs backtest.
2. Identify the biggest deviation (execution, regime, psychology).
3. Fix one thing.
4. If pass → micro live at 5–10% of intended capital.
5. Scale quarterly only if metrics hold.
6. If fail → return to paper/backtest; do not force it.
```

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal

**Purpose:** A reusable framework for diagnosing any market crisis — past, present or
future — instead of memorising headlines.

> A crisis is not a single event. It is a **process** with preconditions, a trigger,
> transmission, forced selling, a policy response and a repair phase. If you can place
> the current event on this map, you can act with a plan instead of panic.

---

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 1. The theoretical base (in plain language)
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 1. The theoretical base (in plain language)
1. The theoretical base (in plain language)

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 1. The theoretical base (in plain language) > 1.1 Minsky's instability hypothesis
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 1. The theoretical base (in plain language) > 1.1 Minsky's instability hypothesis
1.1 Minsky's instability hypothesis

Hyman Minsky argued that **stability breeds instability**:

1. A genuine boom makes investors confident.
2. Confidence becomes leverage.
3. Leverage becomes speculation.
4. Speculation becomes Ponzi finance (cash flow cannot even pay interest).
5. A small shock forces asset sales.
6. The system deleverages violently.

**Translation:** the most dangerous time is not when things are bad; it is when
things have been good for too long and everyone is prepared for more good.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 1. The theoretical base (in plain language) > 1.2 Kindleberger's anatomy
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 1. The theoretical base (in plain language) > 1.2 Kindleberger's anatomy
1.2 Kindleberger's anatomy

Charles Kindleberger described bubbles as a sequence:

```
Displacement → Credit expansion → Euphoria → Overtrading
→ Financial distress → Revulsion → Panic → Rescue
```

**Displacement** is a real change (railways, internet, AI, liberalisation). **Credit**
turns it into a bubble. **Euphoria** makes valuation irrelevant. **Revulsion** makes
the same asset untouchable.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 1. The theoretical base (in plain language) > 1.3 Reflexivity
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 1. The theoretical base (in plain language) > 1.3 Reflexivity
1.3 Reflexivity

George Soros's point: prices do not just reflect fundamentals; they **change**
fundamentals. Rising stock prices make it easier to raise capital, which improves the
business, which justifies higher prices — until the loop reverses.

**Indian example:** a rising NBFC stock lowers its cost of capital and helps it grow.
When the stock falls, funding dries up, growth stops, and the fall becomes
self-fulfilling (IL&FS, DHFL).

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 1. The theoretical base (in plain language) > 1.4 Debt-deflation
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 1. The theoretical base (in plain language) > 1.4 Debt-deflation
1.4 Debt-deflation

Irving Fisher's insight: when debt is high and prices fall, the **real burden of debt
rises**. Borrowers sell assets to repay, pushing prices lower, making debt even heavier.

**This is why solvency crises (2008) take years, while valuation crises (2000) recover
faster.**

---

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 1 — Preconditions (the vulnerability)
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 1 — Preconditions (the vulnerability)
Stage 1 — Preconditions (the vulnerability)

Ask: **what is the hidden fragility?**

Common preconditions:

- Leverage (margin, bank loans, carry trades, off-balance-sheet).
- Maturity mismatch (short-term funding for long-term assets).
- Currency mismatch (borrow in USD, earn in INR).
- Concentration (one sector, one stock, one counterparty).
- Valuation extreme (price depends on perpetual growth).
- Regulatory blind spot (shadow banking, unregulated products).
- Narrative dependence ("this time is different").
- Policy complacency (too easy for too long).

**Trading question:** if a shock hits, who is forced to sell?

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 2 — Trigger (the match)
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 2 — Trigger (the match)
Stage 2 — Trigger (the match)

The trigger is often small relative to the reaction:

| Crisis | Trigger | Precondition |
|---|---|---|
| 1929 | October panic | Margin leverage, weak banks |
| 1987 | Program selling | Portfolio insurance, thin liquidity |
| 1992 India | Bank receipt scam exposed | Settlement loophole, leverage |
| 1997 Asia | Thai baht devaluation | USD short-term debt |
| 2000 | Dotcom earnings miss | Valuation bubble |
| 2008 | Lehman failure | Housing leverage, shadow banking |
| 2013 India | Fed taper talk | CAD, FPI dependence |
| 2018 India | IL&FS default | NBFC asset-liability mismatch |
| 2020 | COVID | Global supply/demand shock |
| 2025 | Tariffs | Trade dependence, valuation |
| 2026 | Iran war | Energy dependence, inflation |

**Rule:** the trigger explains the **timing**, not the **size**. The size is explained
by the precondition.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 3 — Transmission (the spread)
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 3 — Transmission (the spread)
Stage 3 — Transmission (the spread)

How does the shock reach the real economy and other markets?

| Channel | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Discount rate** | Higher rates → lower present value | 2022 tech de-rating |
| **Earnings** | Demand/cost shock → lower profits | 2008, 2020 |
| **Liquidity** | Buyers disappear; margin calls | 1987, 2008 |
| **Credit** | Banks stop lending; spreads widen | 2008, 2018 NBFC |
| **Currency** | Capital flight; import inflation | 1991, 1997, 2013 |
| **Commodity** | Oil/food shock → inflation | 1973, 2022, 2026 |
| **Confidence** | Spending/investment delayed | 2011, 2016 Brexit |
| **Political** | Policy uncertainty; regime change | 2004, 2014, 2024 |

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 4 — Liquidity spiral (the forced selling)
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 4 — Liquidity spiral (the forced selling)
Stage 4 — Liquidity spiral (the forced selling)

This is where markets become **non-fundamental**:

- Margin calls force hedge funds to sell anything liquid.
- Redemptions force mutual funds to sell.
- Risk-parity/vol-target funds de-lever automatically.
- Banks cut credit lines.
- Even "safe" assets are sold to raise cash.
- Correlations go to 1; diversification temporarily fails.

**Signs:** bid-ask spreads widen, volume spikes on down days, good news is ignored,
gold and bonds can fall together with stocks (dash for cash).

**Trading rule:** never assume you can exit at your stop in a liquidity spiral. Size
for gap risk.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 5 — Policy response (the extinguisher)
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 5 — Policy response (the extinguisher)
Stage 5 — Policy response (the extinguisher)

Policy tools:

| Tool | Who | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Rate cuts | Central bank | Lower discount rate, support demand |
| Liquidity injection | Central bank | Stop funding runs |
| QE/asset purchases | Central bank | Compress risk premia |
| Fiscal stimulus | Government | Support income/demand |
| Bank recapitalisation | Government | Restore solvency/trust |
| Deposit guarantees | Government | Stop bank runs |
| Regulatory forbearance | Regulator | Buy time (can backfire) |
| Tariff/trade policy | Government | Can worsen or resolve |
| Ceasefire/diplomacy | Governments | Remove the trigger |

**Key question:** is the response **fast, large and credible**? If yes, the bottom is
usually closer. If no, the crisis drags.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 6 — Bottoming (the process)
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 6 — Bottoming (the process)
Stage 6 — Bottoming (the process)

A bottom is a **process**, not a day. Typical signs:

- Bad news stops producing new lows.
- Volatility peaks and starts falling.
- Breadth improves (fewer stocks making lows).
- Volume dries up on retests.
- Credit spreads stabilise.
- Policy response is believed.
- Currency/oil stabilises.

**Do not confuse a bounce with a bottom.** In solvency crises, the first 10–20% rally
often fails.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 7 — Repair (the rebuild)
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 7 — Repair (the rebuild)
Stage 7 — Repair (the rebuild)

This is the slow part:

- Banks repair capital and resume lending.
- Households/corporates deleverage.
- Earnings stabilise.
- Confidence returns.
- Regulation is rewritten.
- Leadership changes.

**India example:** after 2008, the Sensex bottomed in March 2009, but credit growth
and capex took years to normalise. The index recovered by 2014; the economy felt the
crisis for longer.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 8 — Recovery (the new cycle)
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 2. The 8-stage crisis lifecycle > Stage 8 — Recovery (the new cycle)
Stage 8 — Recovery (the new cycle)

Recovery is not a return to the old normal. It is a **new leadership**:

- 2000: tech → energy/financials/EM.
- 2008: financials → US tech/QE beneficiaries.
- 2020: travel/energy → digital/semis/clean energy.
- 2022: long-duration tech → energy/value/cash flow.
- 2026: globalisation winners → domestic demand/defense/energy security.

**Rule:** the recovery rarely rewards the stocks that led the bubble.

---

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 1 — Valuation bubble
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 1 — Valuation bubble
Type 1 — Valuation bubble

- **What:** prices discount implausible growth; no systemic leverage.
- **Examples:** 2000 dotcom, 2021 growth/meme, parts of 2024–25 AI.
- **Drawdown:** 20–50% for the index; 70–90% for the bubble leaders.
- **Recovery:** 2–5 years; depends on earnings.
- **Playbook:** avoid the bubble; own cash-flow-positive quality; wait for valuation
  support.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 2 — Credit/leverage/solvency crisis
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 2 — Credit/leverage/solvency crisis
Type 2 — Credit/leverage/solvency crisis

- **What:** borrowers cannot repay; banks/counterparties lose trust.
- **Examples:** 1929, 2008, 1992 India, 2018 IL&FS.
- **Drawdown:** 40–60%+; long recovery.
- **Recovery:** 5–10 years; requires recapitalisation and reform.
- **Playbook:** cash, quality, avoid leveraged financials; wait for credit spreads to
  stabilise.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 3 — Currency/BOP crisis
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 3 — Currency/BOP crisis
Type 3 — Currency/BOP crisis

- **What:** fixed/pegged currency, short-term foreign debt, reserves drain.
- **Examples:** 1991 India, 1997 Asia, 1994 Mexico, 2013 taper.
- **Drawdown:** 20–60%; currency collapse amplifies.
- **Recovery:** 1–3 years with IMF/policy adjustment.
- **Playbook:** avoid foreign-currency leverage; exporters/IT can benefit; domestic
  demand names can suffer.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 4 — Commodity/oil/inflation shock
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 4 — Commodity/oil/inflation shock
Type 4 — Commodity/oil/inflation shock

- **What:** supply disruption raises input costs; central banks tighten.
- **Examples:** 1973, 1979, 2022, 2026.
- **Drawdown:** 15–45%; depends on policy.
- **Recovery:** 1–3 years; oil must stabilise.
- **Playbook:** energy producers/defense can benefit; consumers/airlines/paints hurt;
  India's CAD/rupee vulnerable.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 5 — Geopolitical/war shock
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 5 — Geopolitical/war shock
Type 5 — Geopolitical/war shock

- **What:** conflict, sanctions, supply-route disruption.
- **Examples:** 1990 Gulf War, 2022 Ukraine, 2025 India–Pakistan, 2026 Iran.
- **Drawdown:** usually 5–20%, unless oil/supply is hit.
- **Recovery:** fast if the war is short and contained; slow if it changes the energy
  regime.
- **Playbook:** don't panic-sell the first headline; assess oil, duration, alliances,
  and policy response.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 6 — Pandemic/health shock
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 6 — Pandemic/health shock
Type 6 — Pandemic/health shock

- **What:** a pathogen disrupts supply and demand simultaneously.
- **Examples:** 1918 flu, 2020 COVID.
- **Drawdown:** 30–40% in weeks.
- **Recovery:** V-shaped if policy is massive; longer if the health system collapses.
- **Playbook:** own liquidity and quality; don't short the policy response.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 7 — Political/policy shock
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 7 — Political/policy shock
Type 7 — Political/policy shock

- **What:** election surprise, tax change, regulation, tariff, demonetisation.
- **Examples:** 2004 India election, 2016 Brexit, 2016 demonetisation, 2025 tariffs.
- **Drawdown:** 5–20%; sector-specific can be worse.
- **Recovery:** depends on whether the policy is reversed or absorbed.
- **Playbook:** trade the **sector impact**, not the headline; gap risk is high.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 8 — Fraud/governance crisis
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 8 — Fraud/governance crisis
Type 8 — Fraud/governance crisis

- **What:** accounting fraud, diversion, related-party abuse, auditor failure.
- **Examples:** 1992 Harshad Mehta, 2001 Ketan Parekh, 2009 Satyam, 2018 PNB,
  2023 Adani–Hindenburg (allegations).
- **Drawdown:** stock-specific 50–90%; sector contagion possible.
- **Recovery:** company-specific; some never recover.
- **Playbook:** cash flow, pledge, auditor, related-party checks; position-size for
  governance risk.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 9 — Microstructure/flash crash
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 9 — Microstructure/flash crash
Type 9 — Microstructure/flash crash

- **What:** trading plumbing fails; liquidity disappears; prices gap.
- **Examples:** 1987, 2010 flash crash, 2024 yen carry (partly).
- **Drawdown:** 5–20% intraday; usually fast recovery.
- **Recovery:** hours to months, depending on structural fixes.
- **Playbook:** avoid market orders in thin liquidity; use limits; size for gaps.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 10 — Natural disaster/climate
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 3. The 10 crisis types > Type 10 — Natural disaster/climate
Type 10 — Natural disaster/climate

- **What:** earthquake, flood, cyclone, drought, pandemic-like supply shock.
- **Examples:** 2004 tsunami, 2011 Japan earthquake, 2025 India–Pakistan? (not climate),
  monsoon failures.
- **Drawdown:** local/sector-specific; macro if agriculture/energy hit.
- **Recovery:** rebuild spending can be stimulative.
- **Playbook:** assess insurance, supply chains, rural demand, inflation.

---

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 4. Transmission matrix
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 4. Transmission matrix
4. Transmission matrix

| Shock | Earnings | Discount rate | Liquidity | Currency | Credit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rate hike | ↓ | ↑ | ↓ | ↑ (INR?) | ↓ |
| Oil spike | ↓ | ↑ | – | ↓ | – |
| War | ↓ (local) | ↑ | ↓ | ↓ | – |
| Pandemic | ↓↓ | ↓ | ↓↓ | ↓ | ↑ stress |
| Tariff | ↓ (exporters) | – | – | ↓ | – |
| Fraud | ↓ (stock) | – | – | – | ↑ (bank) |
| Election | ↔ | ↔ | ↔ | ↔ | ↔ |
| Taper tantrum | ↔ | ↑ | ↓ | ↓ | ↓ |
| Credit crisis | ↓↓ | ↓ | ↓↓ | ↓ | ↑↑ |

**Use:** for any event, mark which columns are hit. If only "sentiment" is hit, it is
usually a trade. If earnings + credit + liquidity are hit, it is a regime change.

---

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 5. India-specific anatomy
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 5. India-specific anatomy
5. India-specific anatomy

India's crises usually combine **global weather** with **domestic plumbing**.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 5. India-specific anatomy > 5.1 The five India channels
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 5. India-specific anatomy > 5.1 The five India channels
5.1 The five India channels

```
1. Oil (Brent) ──→ CPI, CAD, rupee, OMC margins
2. Rupee (USD/INR) ──→ import inflation, FPI flows, IT/pharma earnings
3. FPI flows ──→ large-cap liquidity, index gaps, small-cap contagion
4. RBI policy ──→ rate-sensitives, credit growth, currency
5. Domestic politics/policy ──→ capex, welfare, taxes, regulation
```

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 5. India-specific anatomy > 5.2 The India crisis checklist
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 5. India-specific anatomy > 5.2 The India crisis checklist
5.2 The India crisis checklist

- [ ] Brent above its 200-day average and rising?
- [ ] USD/INR making new highs?
- [ ] FPI selling equities/debt for 3+ weeks?
- [ ] RBI hiking or defending the rupee?
- [ ] Credit spreads/NBFC funding costs widening?
- [ ] Election/budget/regulatory event within 30 days?
- [ ] Small-cap breadth deteriorating before the index?
- [ ] VIX rising while the index is near highs?

**If 3+ are true, reduce risk. If 5+ are true, treat it as a regime change.**

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 5. India-specific anatomy > 5.3 Why India sometimes decouples
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 5. India-specific anatomy > 5.3 Why India sometimes decouples
5.3 Why India sometimes decouples

- Domestic consumption is ~60–70% of GDP.
- RBI has reserves and tools.
- DII flows (SIPs) absorb FPI selling.
- Corporate balance sheets are healthier than in 2008.
- But: oil, rupee and FPI can still force a sharp correction.

**Decoupling is a degree, not a binary.**

---

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 6. Early-warning dashboard
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 6. Early-warning dashboard
6. Early-warning dashboard

Use a simple 1–5 score for each; total 0–30.

| Indicator | 1 (calm) | 3 (caution) | 5 (crisis) |
|---|---|---|---|
| VIX | <15 | 20–30 | >40 |
| Credit spreads | Tight | Widening | Blown out |
| Yield curve | Normal | Flat/inverted | Repricing violently |
| USD/INR | Stable | 3–5% depreciation | >10% depreciation |
| Brent | Stable | +20% | +50%+ |
| Breadth | Healthy | Narrowing | 80%+ stocks below 200DMA |
| FPI flows | Inflows | Outflows | Sustained heavy outflows |
| Bank/NBFC funding | Normal | Cost rising | Access lost |
| Policy | Predictable | Uncertain | Emergency mode |
| News tone | Normal | Negative | Capitulation |

**How to use:** score weekly. A rising score is a **risk-reduction signal**, not a
prediction. You do not need to know the future to manage exposure.

---

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 7. Severity and duration model
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 7. Severity and duration model
7. Severity and duration model

| Severity | Drawdown | Typical recovery | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Correction** | 5–10% | Weeks–months | 2018, 2024 election |
| **Bear market** | 10–20% | 6–18 months | 2011, 2013, 2022 |
| **Severe bear** | 20–40% | 1–3 years | 1987, 2020, 2025 |
| **Crisis** | 40–60% | 3–7 years | 2008, 1992 |
| **Systemic** | 60%+ | 7–15 years | 1929, Japan 1990 |

**But:** drawdown alone is not the classifier. A 20% fall in a solvency crisis is
worse than a 35% fall in a pandemic with massive policy support.

---

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 8. Case studies > 8.1 1929 — the policy-error depression
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 8. Case studies > 8.1 1929 — the policy-error depression
8.1 1929 — the policy-error depression

| Stage | What happened |
|---|---|
| Preconditions | Margin leverage, weak banks, gold standard |
| Trigger | October 1929 panic |
| Transmission | Bank failures, deflation, trade war |
| Policy | Tight money, Smoot–Hawley tariffs |
| Bottom | July 1932 |
| Recovery | 1954 |
| Lesson | **Policy error converts a crash into a depression.** |

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 8. Case studies > 8.2 1987 — the plumbing crash
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 8. Case studies > 8.2 1987 — the plumbing crash
8.2 1987 — the plumbing crash

| Stage | What happened |
|---|---|
| Preconditions | Portfolio insurance, program trading, high valuations |
| Trigger | Cascading sell orders |
| Transmission | Liquidity gap, global contagion |
| Policy | Central bank liquidity |
| Bottom | Weeks |
| Recovery | ~2 years |
| Lesson | **Microstructure can break without a recession.** |

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 8. Case studies > 8.3 1997 — the currency mismatch
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 8. Case studies > 8.3 1997 — the currency mismatch
8.3 1997 — the currency mismatch

| Stage | What happened |
|---|---|
| Preconditions | Dollar pegs, short-term foreign debt, property bubbles |
| Trigger | Thai baht devaluation |
| Transmission | Capital flight, currency collapse, IMF austerity |
| Policy | IMF packages, structural reform |
| Bottom | 1998 |
| Recovery | 1999–2000 |
| Lesson | **Currency mismatch + leverage = contagion.** |

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 8. Case studies > 8.4 2000 — the valuation bubble
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 8. Case studies > 8.4 2000 — the valuation bubble
8.4 2000 — the valuation bubble

| Stage | What happened |
|---|---|
| Preconditions | Dotcom narrative, IPO mania, no earnings |
| Trigger | Earnings misses, Fed tightening |
| Transmission | Tech de-rating, telecom capex collapse |
| Policy | Fed cuts to 1% |
| Bottom | October 2002 |
| Recovery | 2007 (S&P); 2015 (Nasdaq) |
| Lesson | **Narrative without cash flow is fragile.** |

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 8. Case studies > 8.5 2008 — the solvency crisis
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 8. Case studies > 8.5 2008 — the solvency crisis
8.5 2008 — the solvency crisis

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 9. False alarms vs real crises
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 9. False alarms vs real crises
9. False alarms vs real crises

| Signal | False alarm | Real crisis |
|---|---|---|
| Headline | Expected/leaked | Surprise |
| Breadth | Index falls, breadth holds | Breadth deteriorates |
| Credit | Spreads stable | Spreads blow out |
| Currency | Stable | Sharp depreciation |
| Policy | No response needed | Emergency response |
| Earnings | No change | Guidance cuts |
| Recovery | Days | Weeks/months |

**Rule:** one indicator is noise; a **cluster** is a crisis.

---

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 10. Crisis playbook (one page) > Before a crisis
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 10. Crisis playbook (one page) > Before a crisis
Before a crisis

- [ ] Cash buffer (3–6 months expenses; 10–20% portfolio dry powder).
- [ ] Position sizes sized for gap risk, not just stop distance.
- [ ] No leveraged positions in illiquid names.
- [ ] Written invalidation for every position.
- [ ] Event calendar (RBI, budget, elections, expiry).

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 10. Crisis playbook (one page) > During a crisis
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 10. Crisis playbook (one page) > During a crisis
During a crisis

- [ ] Score the event with the six-factor triage.
- [ ] Identify the crisis type (valuation/credit/currency/commodity/war/policy).
- [ ] Check the policy response (fast/large/credible?).
- [ ] Reduce risk if the transmission hits earnings + credit + liquidity.
- [ ] Do not average down leveraged positions.
- [ ] Keep a watchlist of quality names; wait for the bottom checklist.

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 10. Crisis playbook (one page) > After a crisis
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 10. Crisis playbook (one page) > After a crisis
After a crisis

- [ ] Wait for credit/volatility/breadth stabilisation.
- [ ] Scale in gradually; don't all-in on the first bounce.
- [ ] Expect new leadership.
- [ ] Journal the decision quality, not just the P&L.
- [ ] Update your rules for the next regime.

---

chunks.title: 🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 11. Teluglish takeaway
chunks.text:
🧬 Crisis Anatomy — How Markets Break and Heal > 11. Teluglish takeaway
11. Teluglish takeaway

- Crisis ki **trigger** okati, **vulnerability** okati. War/tariff vachindi ani kaadu
  market padindi — leverage/liquidity/valuation ekkuva undi ani padindi.
- 8 stages: preconditions → trigger → transmission → liquidity spiral → policy →
  bottom → repair → recovery. Ee stage telisthe, panic tagguthundi.
- Policy response fast + large + credible aithe bottom early; slow/small aithe years.
  2008 vs 2020 ee difference.
- India lo oil, rupee, FPI, RBI — ee naalugu first chudandi. 3+ red flags unte risk
  tagginchandi; "no trade" kuda oka plan.

| Item | Detail |

| **Context** | US Civil War cuts off cotton supply to Britain |
| **Boom** | Indian cotton exports and prices surge; Bombay merchants make fortunes |
| **Bust** | 1865: US supply returns; cotton prices collapse; speculative fortunes wiped out |
| **Lesson** | A **supply shock** creates a boom; the end of the shock creates the bust. |

The cotton boom financed Bombay's broker community and created the speculative
culture that eventually formalised as the BSE.

chunks.title: Era 2 — 1947–1991: The Controlled Market > 2.5 The 1991 balance-of-payments crisis
chunks.text:
Era 2 — 1947–1991: The Controlled Market > 2.5 The 1991 balance-of-payments crisis
2.5 The 1991 balance-of-payments crisis

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Date** | 1991 |
| **Trigger** | Gulf War oil spike, remittance drop, fiscal deficit, loss of confidence |
| **Vulnerability** | Fixed exchange rate, import dependence, low reserves |
| **Severity** | Reserves fell to ~$1.1–1.2 billion — weeks of imports |
| **Policy** | Rupee devaluation (July 1991), LPG reforms (24 July 1991), IMF loan, gold pledge |
| **Market** | Sensex volatile; confidence restored gradually |
| **Lesson** | **BOP crises force regime change.** 1991 is the birth of modern India. |

**Era 2 takeaway:** 1947–91 was a **controlled, low-liquidity market**. The 1991 crisis
was the hinge: without it, there would be no NSE, no FIIs, no modern derivatives market.

Era 3 — 1991–2000: Liberalisation and the Modern Market > 3.1 The 1992 Harshad Mehta scam
3.1 The 1992 Harshad Mehta scam

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Date** | Exposed April 1992 |
| **Modus operandi** | Bank receipts (BRs) used to divert bank funds into equities; fake cheques; circular trading |
| **Size** | ~₹5,000 crore (some estimates higher) |
| **Market impact** | Sensex fell **12.77% on 28 April 1992**; roughly halved over the following year |
| **Reform** | SEBI Act 1992 (statutory powers); NSE incorporated November 1992 |
| **Lesson** | **Leverage + settlement loopholes + weak supervision = systemic fraud.** |

chunks.title: Era 3 — 1991–2000: Liberalisation and the Modern Market > 3.1 The 1992 Harshad Mehta scam > Why it matters
chunks.text:
Era 3 — 1991–2000: Liberalisation and the Modern Market > 3.1 The 1992 Harshad Mehta scam > Why it matters
Why it matters

The scam was not just a broker cheating. It exposed a **settlement system** where
bank receipts could be used as collateral without verification. The fix was structural:
electronic trading, anonymous matching, and a stronger regulator.

**Why NSE won:** transparency, anonymity, national access, standardised margining,
and a clean derivatives ecosystem. Within a year, turnover exceeded BSE's.

chunks.text:
Era 3 — 1991–2000: Liberalisation and the Modern Market > 3.6 The 2000–01 dotcom bust and Ketan Parekh scam
3.6 The 2000–01 dotcom bust and Ketan Parekh scam

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Peak** | Sensex ~6,178 (February 2000) |
| **Trigger** | Global dotcom bust; Ketan Parekh pump-and-dump in K-10 stocks; bank funding |
| **Vulnerability** | Leverage, illiquid stocks, circular trading, weak risk controls |
| **Impact** | Sensex fell to ~2,594 by September 2001 (−58%); tech/media stocks collapsed |
| **Policy** | SEBI ban on Parekh; UTI US-64 crisis; JPC; settlement reforms |
| **Recovery** | 2003–04 |
| **Lesson** | **Illiquid stocks + leverage + circular trading = trap.** The exit is always smaller than the entry. |

**Era 3 takeaway:** 1991–2000 created the modern market: **SEBI, NSE, FIIs, demat,
derivatives**. It also created the modern scam template: leverage + opacity +
a charismatic operator.

India's wars and security shocks
India's wars and security shocks

India's wars are usually **short for the equity market** — unless they change the
oil/fiscal regime. The bigger effects come through defense spending, inflation,
foreign aid/sanctions and currency.

chunks.title: Seven India-specific lessons
chunks.text:
Seven India-specific lessons
Seven India-specific lessons

1. **Oil is the invisible tax.** Every Gulf war is an Indian inflation event.
2. **The rupee is a risk gauge.** Sharp depreciation = FPI outflows + import inflation.
3. **Elections create gaps.** Exit polls are not results; size for gap risk.
4. **Scams are a feature of weak plumbing.** Follow the funding, not the narrative.
5. **Regulation lags innovation.** SEBI's rules change the game after the damage.
6. **Domestic demand is a cushion, not a shield.** Global liquidity still matters.
7. **Recovery is led by quality, not by the most beaten-down stock.** The old leader
   rarely leads the next cycle.

chunks.title: 📰 News Types — A Trader's Impact Map
chunks.text:
📰 News Types — A Trader's Impact Map
📰 News Types — A Trader's Impact Map

**Purpose:** Convert any headline into a structured impact assessment. Not every news
item deserves a trade; this file helps you decide **what matters, how it transmits,
and what to do** — without predicting the future.

> **Core idea:** News moves markets through **earnings, discount rate, liquidity,
> currency, credit and risk appetite**. If a headline does not touch at least two of
> these, it is probably noise.

---

chunks.title: 📰 News Types — A Trader's Impact Map > Part 1 — The six-factor triage
chunks.text:
📰 News Types — A Trader's Impact Map > Part 1 — The six-factor triage
Part 1 — The six-factor triage

Score each factor 1–5. Total 6–30.

| Factor | 1 | 3 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Surprise** | Expected/leaked | Partly expected | Complete surprise |
| **Breadth** | One stock | One sector | Whole market/system |
| **Duration** | One day | Weeks | Months/regime change |
| **Policy response** | None needed | Some response | Emergency response |
| **Liquidity** | Deep/normal | Thinning | Frozen |
| **Currency/credit** | Stable | Mild stress | Blown out |

**Interpretation:**

- **6–10:** noise; don't trade the headline.
- **11–17:** tradeable event; use a defined-risk plan.
- **18–24:** regime risk; reduce exposure, hedge, or wait.
- **25–30:** crisis; capital preservation first.

---

chunks.title: 📰 News Types — A Trader's Impact Map > Part 2 — Macro news > 1. Monetary policy (RBI / Fed)
chunks.text:
📰 News Types — A Trader's Impact Map > Part 2 — Macro news > 1. Monetary policy (RBI / Fed)
1. Monetary policy (RBI / Fed)

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **What** | Repo rate, reverse repo, CRR, SLR, liquidity, QE/QT, forward guidance |
| **First-order** | Rate-sensitives re-rate; bond yields move; currency moves |
| **Second-order** | Credit growth, earnings, FPI flows, valuation |
| **India sensitivity** | Very high — banks, NBFCs, auto, real estate, capex |
| **Key nuance** | The **direction** matters less than the **surprise vs expectations** |
| **Playbook** | Trade the rate-sensitive basket; avoid leverage into the event; check guidance |
| **Mistake** | Assuming a cut is always bullish — a cut due to a recession can be bearish |

**Example:** RBI's 2026 hawkish turn after the oil shock pressured rate-sensitives,
even though domestic growth was strong.

chunks.title: 📰 News Types — A Trader's Impact Map > Part 2 — Macro news > 2. Inflation (CPI / WPI / core)
chunks.text:
📰 News Types — A Trader's Impact Map > Part 2 — Macro news > 2. Inflation (CPI / WPI / core)
2. Inflation (CPI / WPI / core)

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **What** | Consumer price index, wholesale price index, food/fuel/core |
| **First-order** | Rate expectations; bond yields; currency |
| **Second-order** | Margins, consumption, policy |
| **India sensitivity** | Very high — food inflation is politically sensitive |
| **Key nuance** | **Core** inflation is stickier; food/fuel can be transient |
| **Playbook** | If core rises → hawkish; if food-only → look through unless persistent |
| **Mistake** | Trading the headline CPI without checking base effects |

**Example:** 2026 oil-driven inflation forced RBI to signal hikes, hitting banks and
autos.

chunks.title: 📰 News Types — A Trader's Impact Map > Part 2 — Macro news > 3. Growth (GDP / PMI / IIP)
chunks.text:
📰 News Types — A Trader's Impact Map > Part 2 — Macro news > 3. Growth (GDP / PMI / IIP)

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **What** | GDP, manufacturing/services PMI, industrial production, unemployment |
| **First-order** | Earnings expectations; cyclicals |
| **Second-order** | Policy, flows, currency |
| **India sensitivity** | High — domestic demand is the core story |
| **Key nuance** | PMI is a leading indicator; GDP is lagging/revisions-prone |
| **Playbook** | Strong growth + low inflation = goldilocks; strong growth + high inflation =
  tightening risk |
| **Mistake** | Extrapolating one quarter |

| **Second-order** | Demand, inflation, rating, currency |
| **India sensitivity** | Very high — capex, railways, defense, housing, rural |
| **Key nuance** | The **fiscal deficit path** matters for bond yields and ratings |
| **Playbook** | Map budget announcements to sectors; avoid buying the headline; wait for
  fine print |
| **Mistake** | Buying "budget stocks" before the event and holding through the sell-off |

chunks.title: 📰 News Types — A Trader's Impact Map > Part 2 — Macro news > 5. Taxation

| **Key nuance** | Tariffs are a **tax on consumers** and a **margin shock** for exporters |
| **Playbook** | Map revenue exposure by geography; avoid companies with high US dependence
  until clarity |
| **Mistake** | Assuming a tariff is permanent — policy can be negotiated (2026 India–US
  deal) |

| **India sensitivity** | Very high — oil import bill, IT/pharma benefit |
| **Key nuance** | A weak rupee is **not uniformly bad**: exporters gain, importers lose |
| **Playbook** | Pair trades: long exporters vs importers; watch RBI intervention |
| **Mistake** | Treating currency as a one-way trade |

chunks.text:
📰 News Types — A Trader's Impact Map > Part 3 — Geopolitical news > 11. War / conflict

|---|---|
| **What** | Interstate war, civil war, terrorism, border conflict |
| **First-order** | Oil, gold, defense, VIX |
| **Second-order** | Inflation, supply chains, fiscal, alliances |
| **India sensitivity** | High via oil; medium via trade/remittances |
| **Key nuance** | The market impact depends on **location, oil, duration and alliances** |
| **Playbook** | Don't panic-sell the first headline; assess oil/Hormuz; defense/oil can rally |
| **Mistake** | Assuming every war is a market crash — many are short, contained events |

**Examples:** 1990 Gulf War (oil spike, quick recovery); 2022 Ukraine (inflation
regime); 2025 India–Pakistan (brief risk-off); 2026 Iran (oil shock, fragile recovery).

chunks.title: 📰 News Types — A Trader's Impact Map > Part 9 — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
📰 News Types — A Trader's Impact Map > Part 9 — Common mistakes
Part 9 — Common mistakes

1. **Trading the headline, not the transmission.** Ask: earnings, rates, liquidity,
   currency, credit?
2. **Ignoring expectations.** A "bad" number can be bullish if it was worse than feared.
3. **Confusing a trigger with a cause.** The war is the match; leverage is the fuel.
4. **Over-trading.** Most news is noise.
5. **No invalidation.** If you can't say what proves you wrong, don't trade.
6. **Ignoring costs.** Frequent news trading is taxed and eaten by spreads.
7. **Recency bias.** The last crisis is not the next one.
8. **Assuming policy is permanent.** Tariffs/rules can reverse.
9. **Ignoring currency.** INR moves can dominate equity returns.
10. **No data stamp.** If you don't know the date/source, you don't know the fact.

chunks.title: Module 13 — Market History & News: World + India (1875 → 19 Nov 2026) > The 5-question method (use for every event)
chunks.text:
Module 13 — Market History & News: World + India (1875 → 19 Nov 2026) > The 5-question method (use for every event)
The 5-question method (use for every event)

When any major news breaks, answer these five questions **in writing**:

1. **What changed?** — the fact, not the headline. Date, actor, magnitude.
2. **What is the surprise?** — was it expected? How much is priced in?
3. **What is the transmission?** — earnings, discount rate, liquidity, currency,
   credit, or sentiment?
4. **Who is forced to act?** — margin calls, redemptions, central bank, government,
   regulator. Forced sellers create the extremes.
5. **What would prove me wrong?** — the condition that invalidates your view.

If you cannot answer all five, you have **information**, not an **edge**.

chunks.title: Module 13 — Market History & News: World + India (1875 → 19 Nov 2026) > The 8-stage crisis lifecycle (preview)
chunks.text:
Module 13 — Market History & News: World + India (1875 → 19 Nov 2026) > The 8-stage crisis lifecycle (preview)
The 8-stage crisis lifecycle (preview)

```
Preconditions → Trigger → Transmission → Liquidity spiral
      → Policy response → Bottoming → Repair → Recovery
```

**Preconditions** are the vulnerability. **Trigger** is the match. **Policy response**
is the extinguisher. **Recovery** is the rebuild.

Most beginners focus on the trigger ("war started, market fell"). Professionals focus
on the preconditions ("leverage was high, so the war caused forced selling") and the
policy response ("central bank cut rates and injected liquidity, so the bottom formed").

Full detail in [`CRISIS-ANATOMY.md`](CRISIS-ANATOMY.md).

**Template:** use [`../../templates/news-triage.md`](../../templates/news-triage.md)
to score a live event.

chunks.title: Module 13 — Market History & News: World + India (1875 → 19 Nov 2026) > The India transmission map (preview)
chunks.text:
Module 13 — Market History & News: World + India (1875 → 19 Nov 2026) > The India transmission map (preview)
The India transmission map (preview)

```
Global shock
   ├── Oil ↑        → CPI ↑, CAD ↑, rupee ↓ → OMCs/airlines/paints ↓
   ├── US rates ↑   → FPI outflows, valuation ↓ → large caps ↓
   ├── Risk-off     → VIX ↑, correlations → 1 → small caps ↓ more
   ├── Rupee ↓      → IT/pharma ↑, importers ↓
   └── Domestic policy (RBI/budget/SEBI) → sector rotation
```

India is **domestic-demand driven** most of the time, but it is **oil-and-rupee
sensitive** in a global shock. That is why 2026 was a war-driven inflation story, not
a banking crisis.

chunks.text:
🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position
🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position

**Purpose:** A practical plan for the period **after** a crash: how to tell a bounce
from a bottom, what leads, what lags, how to size, and what to avoid.

> The goal is not to catch the exact bottom. The goal is to **survive the fall, keep
> dry powder, and participate in the repair** without taking ruin risk.

chunks.title: 🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 1. The math of recovery (why drawdowns are asymmetric)
chunks.text:
🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 1. The math of recovery (why drawdowns are asymmetric)
1. The math of recovery (why drawdowns are asymmetric)

| Drawdown | Gain needed to break even |
|---|---|
| −10% | +11.1% |
| −20% | +25.0% |
| −30% | +42.9% |
| −40% | +66.7% |
| −50% | +100% |
| −60% | +150% |
| −70% | +233% |
| −80% | +400% |

**Implication:** avoiding a −50% drawdown is worth more than chasing a +50% rally.
Capital preservation is not conservative; it is mathematically optimal.

chunks.text:
🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 2. The four recovery shapes > V-shape — violent fall, violent rise
V-shape — violent fall, violent rise

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Example** | 2020 COVID, 2001 9/11, 1987 |
| **Cause** | Exogenous shock + fast, massive policy |
| **Feel** | "I'll wait for confirmation" → market is already up 20% |
| **Strategy** | Don't short the bounce; buy quality on the first higher low; use tranches |
| **Risk** | Chasing the first 10% and then getting a retest |

| Feature | Detail |

| **Cause** | Solvency/credit crisis; balance-sheet repair |

chunks.title: 🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 5. The bottom checklist
chunks.text:
🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 5. The bottom checklist
5. The bottom checklist

A durable bottom usually has **at least 4 of 6**:

- [ ] **Policy response** is fast, large and credible.
- [ ] **Credit spreads** stop widening; bank funding normalises.
- [ ] **Volatility** peaks and starts falling.
- [ ] **Breadth** improves (fewer stocks making new lows).
- [ ] **Volume** dries up on retests (selling exhaustion).
- [ ] **Currency/oil/global risk** stabilises.

**Bonus signals:**

- [ ] Insider/promoter buying.
- [ ] Buybacks/dividends increasing.
- [ ] Earnings revisions stabilising.
- [ ] Media sentiment at maximum pessimism.
- [ ] IPO activity dries up (capitulation).

**No checklist = no bottom call.** You can still own quality; you just don't go all-in.

---

chunks.title: 🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 6. The recovery stages (a trader's map) > Stage 1 — Capitulation
chunks.text:
🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 6. The recovery stages (a trader's map) > Stage 1 — Capitulation
Stage 1 — Capitulation

- Panic selling; volume spike; VIX peak.
- Bad news everywhere; no buyers.
- **Action:** protect capital; don't short into panic; build a watchlist.

chunks.text:

- Range-bound; breadth improves; leaders emerge.

chunks.text:

- Trend resumes; earnings improve; flows return.

chunks.text:

Stage 6 — Euphoria

- Valuation stretches; everyone is bullish.
- **Action:** reduce risk; tighten stops; raise cash.

chunks.title: 🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 7. Playbook by participant type > 7.1 Long-term investor (SIP/portfolio)
chunks.text:
🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 7. Playbook by participant type > 7.1 Long-term investor (SIP/portfolio)
7.1 Long-term investor (SIP/portfolio)

| Do | Don't |
|---|---|
| Continue SIPs through the fall | Stop SIPs because of fear |
| Rebalance to target allocation | Let one sector dominate |
| Add quality large caps in tranches | Average down leveraged/illiquid small caps |
| Keep 6–12 months expenses in cash | Use emergency funds to buy stocks |
| Review thesis, not price | Sell everything at the bottom |

**Rule:** if your thesis has not changed and the balance sheet is strong, a lower price
is an opportunity — but only with **gradual** deployment.

chunks.title: 🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 7. Playbook by participant type > 7.2 Swing trader
chunks.text:
🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 7. Playbook by participant type > 7.2 Swing trader
7.2 Swing trader

| Do | Don't |
|---|---|
| Wait for a higher low + trend confirmation | Catch the falling knife |
| Risk 0.5–1% per trade | Increase size to "recover losses" |
| Trade liquid leaders | Trade illiquid small caps |
| Use time stops | Hold a failed breakout "until it comes back" |
| Keep a trade journal | Revenge trade |

**Setup:** failed breakdown → reclaim of key level → higher low → entry with stop below
the low. Target prior supply zone.

chunks.title: 🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 7. Playbook by participant type > 7.3 Options trader
chunks.text:
🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 7. Playbook by participant type > 7.3 Options trader
7.3 Options trader

| Do | Don't |
|---|---|
| Wait for IV to peak before selling premium | Sell naked options in a crisis |
| Use defined-risk spreads | Short strangles in high IV without wings |
| Size by max loss | Size by premium received |
| Avoid expiry-day gambling | Average down short options |
| Check margin/SPAN | Assume liquidity at your strike |

**IV crush:** after a crisis, implied volatility falls; long options lose even if the
market rises slowly. Seller's edge returns **after** the vol peak, not during it.

chunks.title: 🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 7. Playbook by participant type > 7.4 F&O trader
chunks.text:
🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 7. Playbook by participant type > 7.4 F&O trader
7.4 F&O trader

| Do | Don't |
|---|---|
| Cut size 50% in high-vol regimes | Keep pre-crisis position size |
| Use wider stops or stay out | Use tight stops in gap-prone markets |
| Avoid illiquid strikes | Trade far OTM options for "lottery" |
| Monitor margin | Get forced exit |
| Respect SEBI position limits | Ignore regulation changes |

**Rule:** in a crisis, the biggest risk is not being wrong; it is being **forced out**
at the wrong time.

chunks.title: 🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 7. Playbook by participant type > 7.5 Business owner / salaried investor
chunks.text:
🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 7. Playbook by participant type > 7.5 Business owner / salaried investor
7.5 Business owner / salaried investor

- Protect cash flow first; markets are secondary.
- Don't use working capital or loans to buy the dip.
- Keep human capital diversified (skills, income sources).
- Use the crisis to buy quality assets only with surplus cash.

chunks.title: 🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 8. Scaling in — a practical template
chunks.text:
🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 8. Scaling in — a practical template
8. Scaling in — a practical template

Suppose you have ₹10,00,000 and want to deploy 60% into equities after a 25% drawdown.

| Tranche | Trigger | Amount | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Bottom checklist 3/6 | 20% (₹2,00,000) | Start participation |
| 2 | Retest holds / 4–5/6 | 20% (₹2,00,000) | Confirm the low |
| 3 | Trend confirmation (higher high) | 20% (₹2,00,000) | Add to strength |
| Reserve | New shock / retest | 40% (₹4,00,000) | Keep dry powder |

**Rules:**

- Never deploy all at once.
- Keep 6–12 months expenses separate.
- If the thesis breaks, stop; don't average down.
- Size each stock by risk, not by conviction alone.

---

chunks.title: 🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 9. What to avoid in a recovery
chunks.text:
🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 9. What to avoid in a recovery
9. What to avoid in a recovery

1. **Catching the falling knife** — buying because it fell, not because it is strong.
2. **Averaging down leverage** — the fastest route to ruin.
3. **Buying illiquid small caps** — you can't exit when you need to.
4. **Ignoring costs/taxes** — recovery gains are taxed; frequent trading erodes returns.
5. **Revenge trading** — trying to "make back" losses.
6. **Over-diversifying** — 30 stocks is not diversification; it is confusion.
7. **Ignoring currency** — INR depreciation can offset equity gains.
8. **Assuming the old leader leads** — the next cycle has new leadership.
9. **Ignoring policy** — RBI/SEBI/budget can change the game.
10. **No written plan** — improvisation in a crisis is expensive.

---

chunks.text:

```
Oil stabilises → rupee stabilises → RBI pauses/cuts → credit growth improves
```

chunks.text:

chunks.text:

10.3 India-specific risks in recovery

chunks.title: 🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 12. Teluglish takeaway
chunks.text:
🔄 Recovery Playbook — How Markets Heal and How to Position > 12. Teluglish takeaway
12. Teluglish takeaway

- Drawdown math asymmetric: −50% ki +100% kavali. So **capital preserve** cheyadam
  first priority; bottom catch cheyadam second.
- Recovery shape V/U/W/L — policy response, credit, breadth chusi decide cheyandi.
  First bounce ni bottom anukokandi.
- Early recovery lo **quality large caps, banks, rate-sensitives**; late recovery lo
  **capex, small caps**. Old bubble leaders ni marchipondi.
- Tranches lo deploy cheyandi; all-in cheyakandi. "No trade" kuda oka valid decision.

chunks.title: 🌍 World Market Timeline — 1873 → 19 November 2026
chunks.text:
🌍 World Market Timeline — 1873 → 19 November 2026
🌍 World Market Timeline — 1873 → 19 November 2026

**Purpose:** A working reference of the major global booms, crashes, wars, policy
shocks and recoveries that shaped modern markets — and the lessons that still apply
to an Indian trader today.

> **How to read this file**
> - Dates are event dates, not necessarily the exact market top/bottom.
> - Drawdowns are **approximate peak-to-trough** for the named index unless stated.
> - "Recovery" means regaining the prior nominal peak, not adjusting for inflation.
> - Numbers are for **pattern recognition**, not for quoting as live data.
> - Use current exchange/data-provider levels; historical levels are reference only.

chunks.title: Era 1 — 1873–1913: Railroads, Gold and Panics > 1.1 The Panic of 1873 and the Long Depression
chunks.text:
Era 1 — 1873–1913: Railroads, Gold and Panics > 1.1 The Panic of 1873 and the Long Depression
1.1 The Panic of 1873 and the Long Depression

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Date** | May 1873 (Vienna), September 1873 (US) |
| **Trigger** | Collapse of the Vienna Stock Exchange; railroad overbuilding; bank failures |
| **Vulnerability** | Heavy leverage, speculative railway bonds, gold-standard constraints |
| **Impact** | Global depression lasting until ~1879; US railroad bankruptcies; deflation |
| **Recovery** | Years; confidence returned only with debt restructuring and deflation |
| **Lesson** | A credit boom in a productive new technology (railroads) can still become a bubble. |

The 1873 crash is the first truly **global** market crisis of the industrial era. It
shows the template: a transformative technology, easy credit, a euphoric narrative,
then a funding shock. Replace "railroads" with "dotcom" or "AI" and the structure is
recognisable.

| Item | Detail |

chunks.title: Era 1 — 1873–1913: Railroads, Gold and Panics > 1.3 The Panic of 1893

| **Vulnerability** | Fixed exchange-rate discipline (gold standard), no lender of last resort |
| **Impact** | Severe depression; mass unemployment; deflation |
| **Recovery** | Mid-1890s to 1897 |
| **Lesson** | When the monetary system cannot expand liquidity, a recession becomes a depression. |

chunks.title: Era 1 — 1873–1913: Railroads, Gold and Panics > 1.4 The Panic of 1907
chunks.text:
Era 1 — 1873–1913: Railroads, Gold and Panics > 1.4 The Panic of 1907
1.4 The Panic of 1907

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Date** | October 1907 |
| **Trigger** | Failed attempt to corner United Copper; Knickerbocker Trust run |
| **Vulnerability** | Unregulated trust companies, no central bank, fragile interbank market |
| **Impact** | Dow fell roughly 50% from its 1906 high; severe credit squeeze |
| **Recovery** | ~2 years; J.P. Morgan organised private rescues |
| **Policy response** | Federal Reserve Act 1913 — the lender of last resort is born |
| **Lesson** | A liquidity crisis needs a liquidity Backstop. Private rescues are not scalable. |

| 1907 | Panic of 1907 | Led to the Fed |
| 1912 | Titanic sinking | Insurance/confidence shock; not systemic |
| 1913 | Federal Reserve Act | Modern monetary plumbing begins |

**Era 1 takeaway:** Before central banks, **panics were frequent, violent and long**.
The Fed was created because private bankers could not stop a system-wide run.

chunks.text:

chunks.title: Era 2 — 1914–1939: War, Boom, Crash, Depression > 2.4 The 1929 crash
chunks.text:
Era 2 — 1914–1939: War, Boom, Crash, Depression > 2.4 The 1929 crash
2.4 The 1929 crash

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Date** | Peak 3 September 1929; crash 24–29 October 1929 |
| **Trigger** | Margin calls, speculation, tightening, confidence collapse |
| **Vulnerability** | Buying stocks on 10% margin; weak banking system; no deposit insurance |
| **Key days** | Black Thursday (24 Oct), Black Monday (28 Oct, −12.8%), Black Tuesday (29 Oct, −11.7%) |
| **Drawdown** | Dow −89% by July 1932 (381 → 41) |
| **Policy response** | Initially tight money, Smoot–Hawley tariffs (1930), bank failures; later New Deal, Glass–Steagall, SEC (1934) |
| **Recovery** | Nominal peak regained ~November 1954 (25 years) |
| **Lesson** | **Policy error can turn a crash into a depression.** Leverage + bank runs + trade war = long L. |

chunks.title: Era 2 — 1914–1939: War, Boom, Crash, Depression > 2.4 The 1929 crash > Why it matters
chunks.text:
Era 2 — 1914–1939: War, Boom, Crash, Depression > 2.4 The 1929 crash > Why it matters
Why it matters

The 1929 crash is the reference crisis for **debt-deflation**: falling prices make
debts heavier, forcing asset sales, which push prices lower. The recovery only became
durable after:

1. Bank restructuring and deposit insurance.
2. Leaving the gold standard (more monetary freedom).
3. Fiscal expansion (war spending).
4. Stronger regulation (SEC, disclosure, Glass–Steagall).

chunks.title: Era 2 — 1914–1939: War, Boom, Crash, Depression > 2.5 The 1937–38 recession
chunks.text:
Era 2 — 1914–1939: War, Boom, Crash, Depression > 2.5 The 1937–38 recession
2.5 The 1937–38 recession

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Date** | 1937–1938 |
| **Trigger** | Premature fiscal/monetary tightening; policy uncertainty |
| **Impact** | Dow fell ~50%; unemployment surged again |
| **Lesson** | Withdrawing stimulus too early can restart a depression. |

chunks.title: Era 2 — 1914–1939: War, Boom, Crash, Depression > 2.6 World War II (1939–1945)
chunks.text:
Era 2 — 1914–1939: War, Boom, Crash, Depression > 2.6 World War II (1939–1945)
2.6 World War II (1939–1945)

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Market** | War production, controls, rationing; equities bottomed in 1942 |
| **Policy** | Massive fiscal expansion; Bretton Woods (1944) creates the post-war monetary order |
| **Recovery** | Post-war consumer boom; US dominance |
| **Lesson** | Wars are **fiscal shocks** first and **geopolitical shocks** second. The fiscal response often outlasts the war. |

**Era 2 takeaway:** The 1929–45 period is the strongest evidence that **the policy
response is the single biggest determinant of recovery length**. A crash is not a
depression until the banking system and the policy reaction fail.

| **Vulnerability** | Energy dependence, inflation already rising, weak profits |
| **Impact** | Dow −45% (Jan 1973–Dec 1974); UK bear market >70%; global stagflation |
| **Policy** | Tight money to fight inflation; recession |
| **Recovery** | Nominal 1976; real recovery took until the 1980s |

chunks.text:

|---|---|

| **Trigger** | Fed Chair Paul Volcker raises rates aggressively to break inflation |
| **Impact** | Dow −24%; deep recession; Latin American debt crisis (1982) |

**Era 3 takeaway:** The 1970s is the template for a **supply-shock inflation regime**:
oil ↑ → CPI ↑ → rates ↑ → valuations ↓ → recession. The 2022 and 2026 episodes are
close cousins.

chunks.title: Era 4 — 1980–1999: Leverage, Liberalisation and Contagion > 4.1 The 1987 Black Monday > Why it matters
chunks.text:
Era 4 — 1980–1999: Leverage, Liberalisation and Contagion > 4.1 The 1987 Black Monday > Why it matters
Why it matters

Black Monday was not a recession. It was a **plumbing failure**: automated selling
met thin liquidity. The economy kept growing, and the market recovered. This is the
classic **V-shaped microstructure crash** — different from 2008.

chunks.title: Era 5 — 2000–2009: Bubble, Terror, Credit > 5.4 The 2007–09 global financial crisis > The transmission chain
chunks.text:
Era 5 — 2000–2009: Bubble, Terror, Credit > 5.4 The 2007–09 global financial crisis > The transmission chain
The transmission chain

```
Housing bubble → subprime mortgages → CDOs → leverage → mark-to-market losses
→ margin calls → Bear Stearns → Lehman → money market freeze
→ global trade collapse → EM outflows → India: FII selling, rupee fall, credit freeze
```

**India-specific:** The Sensex fell from 21,206 (Jan 2008) to 8,160 (Mar 2009), about
−61%. Recovery to the 2008 peak took until 2014 — roughly six years. FII outflows and
a credit freeze hit mid-caps and real estate especially hard.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Date** | January 2009 |
| **Event** | Chairman confesses to fake cash/receivables |
| **Impact** | Stock collapsed; auditor credibility crisis; regulatory reform |
| **Lesson** | **Cash on the balance sheet is an opinion; cash flow is a fact.** |

**Era 5 takeaway:** 2000–09 gave us the two archetypes: **valuation bust** (dotcom) and
**solvency bust** (GFC). The first recovers when earnings catch up; the second recovers
when the banks are fixed.

chunks.title: Era 7 — 2020–2026: Pandemic, Inflation, War, Tariffs > 7.10 The 2026 Iran war and global oil shock > The 2026 sequence
chunks.text:
Era 7 — 2020–2026: Pandemic, Inflation, War, Tariffs > 7.10 The 2026 Iran war and global oil shock > The 2026 sequence
The 2026 sequence

```
Feb 28: war begins → Hormuz blocked → oil spikes
March: global equity correction → S&P bottom Mar 30
Apr 8: ceasefire → relief rally
Apr 12–13: Islamabad talks fail → naval blockade
Jun 17: US–Iran memorandum → blockade lifted
Jun 28: ceasefire resumes
Jul 8: ceasefire collapses → oil/volatility return
Sep–Oct: Houthi escalation; RBI signals rate hikes
Nov: US midterms → incumbent party loses Congress
```

**Important:** The 2026 recovery was **partial and fragile**, not a clean V. Oil
remained volatile, inflation persisted, and central banks turned hawkish. Do not
assume the April low was the final low.

chunks.title: Wars and markets — a compact table
chunks.text:
Wars and markets — a compact table
| War/conflict | Period | Main transmission | Market outcome | Lesson |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Korean War | 1950–53 | Commodity inflation, US rearmament | Volatile equities; inflation | War spending can be inflationary |
| Vietnam War | 1955–75 | Fiscal expansion, dollar pressure | 1970s inflation; 1973–74 bear | War + easy money = stagflation |
| Yom Kippur/OPEC embargo | 1973 | Oil quadruples | Global bear; stagflation | Oil is the main war channel |
| Soviet–Afghan War | 1979–89 | Oil risk, Cold War | Volcker tightening; EM debt crisis | Geopolitics can force tight money |
| Iran–Iraq War | 1980–88 | Oil volatility, Gulf shipping | Inflation/volatility | Protracted wars keep a risk premium |
| Gulf War | 1990–91 | Oil spike, recession | Quick recovery after victory | Short war = short shock |
| Afghanistan War | 2001 | Risk-off, war spending | Brief sell-off; recovery | Exogenous shock + policy = fast recovery |
| Iraq War | 2003 | Uncertainty, oil | Relief rally | Markets price uncertainty, then resolve |
| Russia–Georgia War | 2008 | Energy, EM risk | Brief risk-off | Small wars rarely change global trends |
| Crimea/Ukraine sanctions | 2014 | Sanctions, ruble, oil | Ruble crisis; EM outflows | Sanctions can outlast the war |
| Russia–Ukraine War | 2022 | Oil/gas, food, inflation | Global tightening; 2022 bear | War can create an inflation regime |
| Israel–Hamas War | 2023 | Oil risk premium, defense | Limited global drawdown | Not every war is an oil shock |
| Red Sea shipping crisis | 2024 | Freight/supply chains | Cost inflation, not a crash | Supply-chain wars are slow-burn |
| India–Pakistan conflict | 2025 | Oil, rupee, sentiment | Brief risk-off; defense rally | Regional war is usually a trade |
| Iran war | 2026 | Hormuz, oil, inflation | Global correction; fragile recovery | War is an inflation shock first |

**Pattern:** wars that hit **oil/shipping** create lasting inflation; wars that stay
local create short risk-off moves. Always ask: *does this change the energy or fiscal
regime?*

- [ ] Operating cash flow consistently below net profit.
- [ ] Receivables growing faster than revenue.
- [ ] Related-party transactions that are hard to explain.
- [ ] Auditor resignation or frequent auditor changes.
- [ ] High promoter pledge.
- [ ] Complex holding structures/off-balance-sheet debt.
- [ ] Sudden CEO/CFO exits.
- [ ] Aggressive revenue recognition or capitalised costs.

**Rule:** fraud is usually visible in the **cash flow statement** before it is visible

chunks.text:

Pattern 3 — Leadership changes after a crisis

- 2000: telecom/tech → energy, financials, emerging markets.
- 2008: financials → US tech, consumer, QE beneficiaries.
- 2020: travel/energy → digital, semiconductors, clean energy.
- 2022: long-duration tech → energy, value, cash-flow.
- 2025–26: tariff/globalisation winners → domestic-demand, defense, energy security.

**Do not marry the old leader.** The recovery is usually led by something that was

Pattern 4 — Policy response is the biggest variable

| Crisis | Policy response | Recovery |
|---|---|---|
| 1929 | Tight money, tariffs | 25 years |
| 1987 | Liquidity, rate cuts | 2 years |
| 2008 | QE, recapitalisation | 5.5 years |
| 2020 | Unlimited QE, fiscal | 6 months |
| 2022 | Fast hikes | 2 years |

**Rule:** When policy is fast, large and credible, the market bottoms earlier. When

chunks.title: Cross-era patterns > Pattern 5 — India's response function is different
chunks.text:
Cross-era patterns > Pattern 5 — India's response function is different
Pattern 5 — India's response function is different

India usually:

- Falls **less** than the world in a global liquidity crisis if reserves are strong.
- Falls **more** in an oil/rupee crisis because of imported inflation and CAD.
- Recovers faster when **domestic earnings** are intact and RBI cuts rates.
- Suffers more when **FPI outflows** coincide with a credit crisis (2008, 2013, 2018).

What to memorise
What to memorise

1. **1929:** leverage + policy error = depression.
2. **1987:** microstructure can crash the market without a recession.
3. **1997:** currency mismatch + short-term debt = contagion.
4. **2000:** narrative without cash flow = de-rating.
5. **2008:** solvency crises take years; banks must be fixed.
6. **2020:** exogenous shock + massive policy = fast V.
7. **2022:** inflation is a valuation shock.
8. **2025:** policy shocks can reverse; don't over-extrapolate.
9. **2026:** war is an inflation shock; ceasefires are tradeable but fragile.
