chunks.title: 01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types
chunks.text:
01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types
01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types

Most arguments about trading are really arguments about **different lenses**.

One trader says "trend following works"; another says "buying support works". They may
both be right — in different regimes, with different holding periods, costs and risk.

This file gives you the full taxonomy so you can place any strategy on the map.

---

chunks.title: 01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 1. Lens 1 — Holding period
chunks.text:
01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 1. Lens 1 — Holding period
1. Lens 1 — Holding period

| Type | Holding time | Decision timeframe | Overnight risk | Cost sensitivity | Typical user |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Scalping** | Seconds–minutes | 1m / 5m | No | Extreme | Full-time / algo |
| **Intraday** | Same session | 5m / 15m | No | High | Active trader |
| **Swing** | 2–10 days | Daily / 60m | Yes | Medium | Job-going trader |
| **Positional** | Weeks–months | Weekly / daily | Yes | Low–medium | Patient trader |
| **Investment** | Years | Monthly / quarterly | Yes | Low | Long-term investor |

**Key point:** holding period is not the same as chart timeframe. A swing trader can
use a 15m chart for entry timing, but the thesis is daily/weekly.

---

chunks.title: 01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 2. Lens 2 — Edge / style
chunks.text:
01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 2. Lens 2 — Edge / style
2. Lens 2 — Edge / style

| Style | Edge source | Works when | Fails when | Typical holding |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Trend following** | Prices persist in a direction | Clear trend, low noise | Choppy range, whipsaw | Weeks–months |
| **Momentum** | Relative strength persists | Broad rally, sector leadership | Sharp reversal, rotation | Weeks–months |
| **Mean reversion** | Overreaction reverses | Range, low volatility | Strong trend, breakdown | Days–weeks |
| **Breakout** | Volatility expands from compression | Expansion, catalyst | False breakout, low volume | Days–weeks |
| **Pullback** | Trend resumes after a pause | Healthy trend | Trend break, deep correction | Days–weeks |
| **Event/news** | Information is mispriced | Clear surprise, liquid market | Gap, ambiguity, crowded trade | Hours–weeks |
| **Arbitrage** | Price difference converges | Liquid, efficient infrastructure | Spread disappears, execution fails | Seconds–days |
| **Quant/systematic** | Statistical regularity | Repeatable, robust edge | Overfit, regime shift | Varies |
| **Market making** | Spread + rebates | High volume, low adverse selection | Toxic flow, latency war | Seconds |
| **Carry** | Yield/roll premium | Stable markets, low vol | Crash, funding squeeze | Weeks–months |
| **Hedging** | Risk reduction | Always, as insurance | Cost drag, basis risk | Varies |
| **Options income** | Theta / implied volatility premium | Range, high IV | Gap, vol spike, trend | Weeks |

chunks.title: 01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 2. Lens 2 — Edge / style
chunks.text:
01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 2. Lens 2 — Edge / style
**Rule:** if you cannot state the edge in one sentence, it is not a style — it is a
hope.

chunks.title: 01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 3. Lens 3 — Instrument / segment (India)
chunks.text:
01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 3. Lens 3 — Instrument / segment (India)
3. Lens 3 — Instrument / segment (India)

| Segment | What it is | Leverage | Settlement | Main cost | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Delivery equity** | Buy shares, hold in demat | No | T+1 (T+0 optional in select stocks) | STT 0.1% both sides, DP charge | Low–medium |
| **Intraday equity** | Square off same day | Yes (broker) | No delivery | STT 0.025% sell, brokerage | High |
| **Futures** | Index/stock futures | Margin | Mark-to-market, expiry | STT 0.02% sell | High |
| **Options** | Calls/puts | Premium/margin | European (index), physical (stock) | STT 0.1% on sell premium | Very high |
| **ETF** | Diversified basket | No | T+1 | Low | Low–medium |
| **Currency** | USDINR etc. | Margin | Exchange-defined | Segment-specific | High |
| **Commodity** | Gold, silver, crude etc. (MCX) | Margin | Exchange-defined | Segment-specific | High |

> Rules change. Lot sizes, weekly expiry, minimum contract size, margin and STT were
> tightened in 2024–25. Use the current SEBI/exchange circular as the source of truth.

**Segment is not style.** A swing view can be expressed through delivery, futures or
options — each with different risk, cost and tax.

---

chunks.title: 01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 4. Lens 4 — Execution
chunks.text:
01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 4. Lens 4 — Execution
4. Lens 4 — Execution

| Execution | Description | Pros | Cons | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Discretionary** | Human judgment with a checklist | Flexible, context-aware | Emotional, inconsistent | Beginners, swing |
| **Systematic** | Written rules, backtested | Consistent, measurable | Overfit risk, regime shift | Intermediate+ |
| **Algo** | Automated execution | Fast, no emotion | Tech/regulatory risk | Quant, intraday |
| **Hybrid** | Rules + human override | Balance | Override can become bias | Most retail |

**Beginner path:** discretionary + checklist → systematic → hybrid/algo only after
100+ logged trades.

---

chunks.title: 01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 5. Lens 5 — Direction
chunks.text:
01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 5. Lens 5 — Direction
5. Lens 5 — Direction

| Direction | Description | Examples | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Long-only** | Buy and hold / buy strength | Delivery, ETF, trend long | Market beta |
| **Long-short** | Long one, short another | Pairs, sector-neutral | Correlation, borrow |
| **Market-neutral** | No net market exposure | Stat arb, index arb | Execution, crowding |
| **Hedged** | Long asset + hedge | Protective put, collar, beta hedge | Basis risk, cost |

Retail traders usually start long-only. Long-short and market-neutral require
derivatives, margin and execution skill.

chunks.title: 01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 8. Common confusions > Trading vs investing
chunks.text:
01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 8. Common confusions > Trading vs investing
Trading vs investing

| Trading | Investing |
|---|---|
| Profits from price movement | Profits from business earnings |
| Holding: minutes to months | Holding: years |
| Edge: setup, flow, catalyst | Edge: quality, valuation, compounding |
| Costs matter a lot | Costs matter less |
| Screen time | Research time |

Both can coexist: **core portfolio** (long-term) + **satellite** (swing/positional).

chunks.title: 01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 8. Common confusions > Style vs segment
chunks.text:
01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 8. Common confusions > Style vs segment
Style vs segment

- "Swing" is a holding period.
- "Futures" is an instrument.
- "Breakout" is an edge.
- "Systematic" is execution.

A trade can be **swing + futures + breakout + systematic + long + directional**.

chunks.title: 01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 8. Common confusions > Strategy vs setup
chunks.text:
01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 8. Common confusions > Strategy vs setup
Strategy vs setup

- **Setup:** a specific pattern/trigger (e.g., breakout-retest).
- **Strategy:** setup + entry + exit + sizing + risk + costs + review.
- **Edge:** the reason the strategy should make money over many trades.

chunks.title: 01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 8. Common confusions > Edge vs indicator
chunks.text:
01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 8. Common confusions > Edge vs indicator
Edge vs indicator

An indicator is a **tool**. An edge is a **reason**. RSI oversold is not an edge unless
you can explain who is forced to sell and why the reaction should repeat.

chunks.title: 01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 8. Common confusions > Timeframe vs holding period
chunks.text:
01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 8. Common confusions > Timeframe vs holding period
Timeframe vs holding period

A 5m chart can be used for a 3-day swing entry. The chart is timing; the holding
period is risk.

chunks.title: 01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 8. Common confusions > Backtest vs live
chunks.text:
01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 8. Common confusions > Backtest vs live
Backtest vs live

A backtest is a **hypothesis test**, not a promise. Live results differ because of
slippage, costs, regime and psychology.

chunks.title: 01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 8. Common confusions > Diversification vs many correlated trades
chunks.text:
01 — The Taxonomy of Trading Types > 8. Common confusions > Diversification vs many correlated trades
Diversification vs many correlated trades

Five bank stocks are not five independent bets. They are one sector bet. Correlation
is the hidden position size.

chunks.text:

Teluglish takeaway

Trading type ni **holding, edge, instrument, execution, direction, risk** — ee six

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading

**Holding period:** seconds to one session
**Edge:** speed, order flow, liquidity, momentum, levels
**Risk:** high to very high
**India fit:** full-time or active traders with low costs and strict discipline

> Intraday trading is not "fast swing trading". It is a different game: the edge is
> small, the costs are large, and the clock is always running.

---

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 1. What scalping actually is
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 1. What scalping actually is
1. What scalping actually is

Scalping tries to capture a **small price move** many times per day.

| Feature | Scalping |
|---|---|
| Holding | Seconds to a few minutes |
| Trades/day | 10–100+ |
| Target | 0.05–0.3% per trade (index/futures) |
| Stop | Tight, often 0.05–0.15% |
| Edge | Spread, order flow, speed, liquidity |
| Main enemy | Costs, slippage, latency, overtrading |
| Who wins | Low-cost, high-skill, often automated |

**Scalping is not a chart pattern.** It is a **microstructure edge**: you are trying
to buy at the bid and sell at the ask, or ride a burst of order flow before it fades.
If your broker, internet or execution is slow, you are the liquidity being harvested.

---

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 2. The cost math that kills most scalpers
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 2. The cost math that kills most scalpers
2. The cost math that kills most scalpers

Assume:

- Capital: ₹1,00,000
- Trades: 10 per day
- Orders: 20 per day (buy + sell)
- Brokerage: ₹20 per order
- Trading days: 250

```
Brokerage = 20 orders × ₹20 = ₹400/day
Annual    = ₹400 × 250 = ₹1,00,000
Cost as % of capital = 100%
```

That is **before** STT, exchange charges, GST, stamp duty and slippage.

Even at ₹10/order:

```
10 trades × 2 orders × ₹10 = ₹200/day
₹200 × 250 = ₹50,000/year = 50% of capital
```

**Implication:** a scalper targeting 0.2% per trade with 0.1–0.3% round-trip cost is
often trading for the broker, not for himself.

**Rule:** target at least **2–3× round-trip cost**. If not, skip the trade.

---

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 3. What a scalper needs
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 3. What a scalper needs
3. What a scalper needs

| Requirement | Why |
|---|---|
| Low brokerage | Cost per trade must be tiny |
| Tight spreads | Slippage eats the edge |
| Liquid instrument | Nifty/Bank Nifty futures, top large caps |
| Fast execution | Latency and order type matter |
| Hard stop + time stop | No hoping, no averaging |
| Daily loss limit | Prevents tilt |
| Journal with slippage | The only way to know the real edge |
| Automation or semi-automation | Human speed is limited |

**Not enough:** a 1m chart, a "strategy" from YouTube, and motivation.

---

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 4. Intraday styles > A. Opening range breakout (ORB)
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 4. Intraday styles > A. Opening range breakout (ORB)
A. Opening range breakout (ORB)

- Define the first 15/30/60-minute range.
- Enter on a close/retest outside the range with volume.
- Stop: other side of the range or ATR-based.
- Target: measured move or trailing.
- Fails in choppy opens and false breakouts.

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 4. Intraday styles > B. VWAP pullback
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 4. Intraday styles > B. VWAP pullback
B. VWAP pullback

- Trend filter: price above VWAP for longs, below for shorts.
- Entry: pullback to VWAP with rejection.
- Stop: below VWAP/swing.
- Target: prior high/low or R-multiple.
- Fails when price chops around VWAP.

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 4. Intraday styles > C. Momentum / gap-and-go
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 4. Intraday styles > C. Momentum / gap-and-go
C. Momentum / gap-and-go

- Gap up/down with news or broad market move.
- Entry: continuation after the first pullback.
- Stop: gap fill or opening range.
- Target: measured move/trailing.
- Fails on gap fill and reversal days.

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 4. Intraday styles > D. Reversal / fade at a level
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 4. Intraday styles > D. Reversal / fade at a level
D. Reversal / fade at a level

- Price reaches a major S/R, previous day high/low, or round number.
- Entry: rejection candle + volume.
- Stop: beyond the level.
- Target: mid-range/VWAP.
- Fails in strong trends; fading strength is dangerous.

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 4. Intraday styles > E. News/event intraday
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 4. Intraday styles > E. News/event intraday
E. News/event intraday

- RBI, budget, earnings, global cues, war headlines.
- First move is often noise; wait for the second move/liquidity.
- Spreads widen; slippage is high.
- Size down or skip if the event is binary.

---

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 5. India-specific mechanics
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 5. India-specific mechanics
5. India-specific mechanics

| Item | What to know |
|---|---|
| **Square-off** | Brokers auto-square off intraday positions before close |
| **Leverage** | Broker-specific; SEBI margin rules apply |
| **STT** | 0.025% on sell side (intraday equity) |
| **Brokerage** | Per order; check the plan |
| **Stamp duty** | 0.003% on buy side (intraday) |
| **Exchange/GST** | Small but real |
| **Circuit limits** | Stocks can lock; you may not exit |
| **F&O ban** | No new positions in banned contracts |
| **Expiry** | Intraday options near expiry have extreme gamma/theta |
| **BTST** | Delivery-based; auction/short-delivery risk |

> Use current broker/exchange rates and margin rules; they change.

---

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 6. BTST and MTF
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 6. BTST and MTF
6. BTST and MTF

| Type | What it is | Main risk |
|---|---|---|
| **BTST** | Buy today, sell tomorrow (delivery-based) | Overnight gap, auction/short delivery |
| **MTF** | Broker funds part of the delivery purchase | Interest cost, leverage, forced liquidation |

**BTST** is not a separate edge; it is a holding-period choice. **MTF** is leverage —
size it like leverage, not like free money. Verify broker/exchange rules and rates.

---

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 7. Risk rules for intraday
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 7. Risk rules for intraday
7. Risk rules for intraday

| Rule | Default |
|---|---|
| Risk per trade | 0.25–0.5% of capital |
| Max daily loss | 1–2% |
| Max open risk | 2–3% |
| Max trades/day | 3–5 (beginner) |
| Stop | Hard stop, no mental stop |
| Time stop | Exit if thesis not working by a set time |
| Event rule | No new position 15–30 min before a major event |
| Tilt rule | Two losses in a row → stop for the day |

**Example:** ₹5,00,000 capital, 0.5% risk = ₹2,500. Entry ₹250, stop ₹247.50 →
risk/unit ₹2.50 → 1,000 shares → position ₹2,50,000. If the stop slips to ₹247,
loss is ₹3,000 (0.6%) — still acceptable, but size for slippage.

---

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 8. Who should avoid intraday
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 8. Who should avoid intraday
8. Who should avoid intraday

- You have a full-time job with meetings.
- You cannot watch the first 60 minutes.
- You trade with borrowed money.
- You have no hard stop discipline.
- You cannot calculate costs.
- You revenge trade after a loss.
- You have less than 6 months of paper/journal experience.

**No trade is a valid answer.** Cash is a position.

---

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 9. 30-trade practice plan
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 9. 30-trade practice plan
9. 30-trade practice plan

| Phase | Trades | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Observe | 5 days | Mark ORB, VWAP, S/R; no trades |
| 2. Paper | 10 | One setup only; journal entry/exit/slippage |
| 3. Micro live | 10 | 0.25% risk; max 2 trades/day |
| 4. Review | 10 | Only continue if expectancy > 0 after costs |

**Metrics to track:** win rate, average R, cost per trade, slippage, MFE/MAE, time of
day, rule adherence.

---

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 10. Common mistakes
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > 10. Common mistakes
10. Common mistakes

- Trading every move instead of one setup.
- Ignoring costs because "the target is small".
- Widening stops to avoid a loss.
- Averaging a losing intraday position.
- Trading illiquid stocks/options.
- Overtrading after a win.
- Revenge trading after a loss.
- Using 1m charts without a higher-timeframe filter.
- Holding an intraday position into a binary event.

---

chunks.title: 02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > Teluglish takeaway
chunks.text:
02 — Scalping & Intraday Trading > Teluglish takeaway
Teluglish takeaway

Scalping lo edge **speed + cost + liquidity**; chart pattern kadu.
₹1 lakh capital, 10 trades/day, ₹20/order → **₹1 lakh/year brokerage** — STT/slippage
kante mundu ne 100% capital.
Intraday lo **hard stop, daily loss limit, time stop** lekapote, one bad day chalu.
Job unte intraday avoid; paper 30 trades tarvata ne small size start cheyandi.

chunks.title: 03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles
chunks.text:
03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles
03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles

**Holding period:** 2 days to several months
**Edge:** trend, momentum, mean reversion, breakout, pullback, catalyst
**Risk:** medium
**India fit:** job-going traders, patient traders, delivery/futures

> Swing trading is the **sweet spot** for most retail traders: enough time to think,
> enough movement to matter, and fewer costs than intraday.

---

chunks.title: 03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 1. Swing trading
chunks.text:
03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 1. Swing trading
1. Swing trading

| Feature | Swing |
|---|---|
| Holding | 2–10 days (sometimes 2–20) |
| Chart | Daily + 60m for timing |
| Edge | Trend continuation, pullback, breakout, range reversal |
| Overnight risk | Yes — gaps, news, global cues |
| Costs | Medium (4–10 trades/month) |
| Screen time | 30–60 min/day |
| Best for | Working professionals, disciplined beginners |

**Main risk:** you are exposed to overnight gaps. A stop at ₹100 can fill at ₹92 after
bad news. Size for the gap, not the ideal stop.

**Event calendar:** earnings, RBI, budget, elections, expiry, global central bank
meetings, war headlines. If you cannot hold through the event, reduce or exit before it.

---

chunks.title: 03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 2. Positional trading
chunks.text:
03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 2. Positional trading
2. Positional trading

| Feature | Positional |
|---|---|
| Holding | Weeks–months |
| Chart | Weekly + daily |
| Edge | Trend + catalyst + fundamental overlay |
| Overnight risk | Yes |
| Costs | Low–medium |
| Screen time | 15–30 min/day |
| Best for | Patient traders, investors with a trading overlay |

Positional trading sits between swing and investment. You may hold through earnings if
the thesis is intact, but you still define invalidation and position size.

**Catalysts:** earnings cycle, capex, order wins, regulatory change, commodity cycle,
index inclusion, promoter action, M&A.

---

chunks.title: 03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 3. Trend following
chunks.text:
03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 3. Trend following
3. Trend following

**Thesis:** prices tend to persist in a direction because of slow information
diffusion, institutional flows and behavioural anchoring.

**Rules (example, not a recommendation):**

- Universe: liquid large/mid caps or index futures.
- Entry: close above 50/200-day high, or 50/200 EMA alignment.
- Stop: 1.5–3× ATR or recent swing.
- Exit: trailing stop, MA cross, or time stop.
- Sizing: risk 0.5–1% per trade; max 5–8 positions.
- Rebalance: weekly/monthly.

**Works:** strong trends, crisis recoveries, commodity cycles.
**Fails:** choppy ranges, whipsaws, sideways indices.
**Key metric:** expectancy after costs, max drawdown, win rate (often 35–45%).

---

chunks.title: 03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 4. Momentum
chunks.text:
03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 4. Momentum
4. Momentum

**Thesis:** winners keep winning for a while — relative strength persists due to flows,
attention and underreaction.

**Implementation:**

1. Rank a universe by 3/6/12-month return.
2. Filter by liquidity and trend.
3. Buy the top decile/quintile; rebalance monthly/quarterly.
4. Exit on rank drop or stop.
5. Hedge with index futures if needed.

**India context:** sector rotation (banks, IT, pharma, auto, capital goods, PSU,
defence, FMCG) can be strong. Momentum works in broad rallies and fails in sharp
reversals.

**Risks:** crowding, high turnover, transaction costs, sudden factor reversal.

---

chunks.title: 03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 5. Mean reversion
chunks.text:
03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 5. Mean reversion
5. Mean reversion

**Thesis:** short-term overreaction reverses toward the mean.

**Common tools:** RSI extremes, Bollinger bands, distance from 20/50 EMA, support/
resistance, VIX spike, breadth washout.

**Rules (example):**

- Regime filter: only in range/low-vol markets, or after a panic washout.
- Entry: oversold + rejection candle at support.
- Stop: below support/ATR.
- Target: mean (20 EMA/VWAP) or prior range high.
- Size: smaller than trend trades; mean reversion can catch falling knives.

**Works:** range markets, panic rebounds, overextended moves.
**Fails:** strong downtrends, structural breaks, fraud/credit events.

**Rule:** never average down a broken thesis. Mean reversion is a trade, not a
marriage.

---

chunks.title: 03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 6. Breakout
chunks.text:
03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 6. Breakout
6. Breakout

**Thesis:** volatility compression resolves into expansion; stops above resistance and
below support fuel the move.

**Setup:**

- Range/box/flag/triangle/consolidation.
- Volume contraction before, expansion on break.
- Entry: close above resistance, or break-retest-hold.
- Stop: below breakout level/ATR.
- Target: measured move/trailing.
- Avoid: low-volume breakouts, wide spreads, event gaps.

**False breakout:** price breaks, fails to hold, and closes back inside. This is often
a reversal signal — and a reminder that breakout trading needs a tight invalidation.

---

chunks.title: 03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 7. Pullback
chunks.text:
03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 7. Pullback
7. Pullback

**Thesis:** in a healthy uptrend, a short pause offers a better risk-reward entry.

**Setup:**

- Trend filter: price above rising 50/200 EMA, higher highs/lows.
- Pullback to 20/50 EMA, Fibonacci 38–62%, prior breakout level, or VWAP.
- Entry: rejection candle/structure hold.
- Stop: below pullback low/ATR.
- Target: prior high/measured move.

**Fails:** when the pullback becomes a trend reversal. The trend filter and stop are
the difference between a pullback trade and catching a falling knife.

---

chunks.title: 03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 8. Comparison
chunks.text:
03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 8. Comparison
8. Comparison

| Style | Holding | Entry trigger | Stop | Best regime | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trend following | Weeks–months | Breakout/MA alignment | ATR/swing | Strong trend | Whipsaw |
| Momentum | Weeks–months | Relative strength rank | Rank drop/stop | Broad rally | Reversal/crowding |
| Mean reversion | Days–weeks | Oversold at support | Below support | Range/panic | Falling knife |
| Breakout | Days–weeks | Range break + volume | Inside range | Expansion | False breakout |
| Pullback | Days–weeks | Dip in uptrend | Below pullback | Healthy trend | Trend break |

---

chunks.title: 03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 9. Position sizing example
chunks.text:
03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 9. Position sizing example
9. Position sizing example

₹5,00,000 capital, 1% risk = ₹5,000.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Entry | ₹250 |
| Stop | ₹235 |
| Risk/unit | ₹15 |
| Quantity | ₹5,000 / ₹15 = 333 shares |
| Position value | 333 × ₹250 = ₹83,250 |
| R:R at target ₹280 | ₹30 / ₹15 = 2R |

If the stock gaps 5% below stop, loss ≈ ₹5,000 + gap slippage. Size for that.

---

chunks.title: 03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 10. Exercises
chunks.text:
03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > 10. Exercises
10. Exercises

1. Mark 20 charts: trend, range, breakout, pullback.
2. Write a one-page rule set for one swing style.
3. Backtest 100 trades with costs and overnight gaps.
4. Compare trend following vs mean reversion on the same 20 charts.
5. Build a position-size sheet for ₹1L, ₹5L and ₹10L capital.
6. Journal 10 paper swing trades, including event exposure.

---

chunks.title: 03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > Teluglish takeaway
chunks.text:
03 — Swing, Positional & Directional Styles > Teluglish takeaway
Teluglish takeaway

Job unte **swing/positional** best; intraday kante cost takkuva, screen time takkuva.
Swing lo main risk **overnight gap** — stop ideal ga fill avvadu, size gap ki adjust cheyandi.
Trend following lo win rate 40% unna, **2R+ payoff** unte expectancy positive avvachu.
Mean reversion lo falling knife jagratha; trend filter + hard stop lekapote danger.

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles

**Holding period:** hours to months (varies by style)
**Edge:** information, price convergence, statistical regularity, spread capture
**Risk:** high for event; low–medium for arbitrage; model risk for quant
**India fit:** event for experienced discretionary traders; arbitrage/quant for
institutional or well-capitalised systematic traders

> These styles look sophisticated, but sophistication is not the same as edge.
> Every one of them has a failure mode that can be larger than the apparent profit.

---

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 1. Event / news trading
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 1. Event / news trading
1. Event / news trading

**Thesis:** markets misprice the probability or magnitude of an event; the re-pricing
creates a trade.

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 1. Event / news trading > Event types
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 1. Event / news trading > Event types
Event types

| Event | Examples | Key question |
|---|---|---|
| **Monetary** | RBI/Fed policy, rate surprises | Is the market priced for it? |
| **Fiscal** | Budget, taxes, subsidies | Who wins/loses? |
| **Earnings** | Results, guidance | Beat/miss vs expectations, not vs last year |
| **Elections** | National/state results | Policy continuity vs change |
| **Geopolitical** | War, sanctions, tariffs | Does it change oil/credit/risk regime? |
| **Pandemic/disaster** | COVID, floods, earthquake | Supply/demand shock, policy response |
| **Regulatory** | SEBI/FDA/CCI decisions | Compliance cost, business model |
| **Corporate** | M&A, demerger, buyback, fraud | Value transfer, governance |
| **Index** | Inclusion/exclusion, rebalancing | Forced flows |
| **Commodity** | OPEC, inventory, monsoon | Supply/demand shock |
| **Technology** | Product cycle, AI capex | Adoption vs valuation |

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 1. Event / news trading > Event study checklist
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 1. Event / news trading > Event study checklist
Event study checklist

1. **What exactly changed?** Fact vs headline.
2. **What was expected?** Consensus/whisper number.
3. **How much is priced in?** Pre-event drift, options IV.
4. **Who is forced to act?** Index funds, hedgers, shorts, retail.
5. **What is the second-order effect?** Suppliers, competitors, currency, rates.
6. **Can I exit?** Liquidity, circuit, gap risk.
7. **What is the invalidation?** Event interpretation changes or price level breaks.

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 1. Event / news trading > Failure modes
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 1. Event / news trading > Failure modes
Failure modes

- Buying the headline after the move (no edge left).
- Holding through a binary event with oversized leverage.
- Ignoring IV crush on options.
- Assuming a "good" event is automatically bullish.
- Confusing a one-day reaction with a trend.

---

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 2. Arbitrage
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 2. Arbitrage
2. Arbitrage

**Thesis:** two related instruments must converge; you capture the difference.

| Arbitrage | Logic | Main risk |
|---|---|---|
| **Cash-futures** | Futures vs spot basis | Basis widens, margin, execution |
| **ETF vs NAV** | ETF price vs underlying basket | Liquidity, creation/redemption |
| **Index arbitrage** | Index futures vs basket | Execution, tracking error |
| **Merger arbitrage** | Target vs deal price | Deal breaks, regulatory risk |
| **Pairs/stat arb** | Relative value of two stocks | Correlation breaks, crowding |
| **Calendar spread** | Different expiries | Liquidity, margin, event |
| **Currency** | Cross-rate/forward mispricing | Funding, capital controls |

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 2. Arbitrage > India-specific notes
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 2. Arbitrage > India-specific notes
India-specific notes

- Stock futures are physically settled; plan for delivery/margin near expiry.
- STT, stamp duty, exchange charges and slippage can erase a thin spread.
- Shorting cash equity intraday is possible, but overnight shorting needs futures/
  securities lending.
- Borrow costs and margin funding matter.
- Index arbitrage is dominated by institutions with low latency and low costs.

**Retail reality:** pure arbitrage is capital-intensive and competitive. If the spread
looks large, ask what risk you are missing.

---

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 3. Market making / HFT
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 3. Market making / HFT
3. Market making / HFT

**Thesis:** earn the spread and rebates by quoting both sides, managing inventory.

| Feature | Market making / HFT |
|---|---|
| Holding | Seconds or less |
| Edge | Spread, queue position, speed, inventory control |
| Requirements | Low latency, infrastructure, risk systems, exchange memberships |
| Main risk | Adverse selection, toxic flow, latency, regulatory |
| Retail fit | Very poor unless you are a technology firm |

**Why retail should not imitate HFT:** you are competing on microseconds with firms
that co-locate, optimize hardware and pay for data. A retail "scalping bot" on a home
internet connection is not in the same game.

---

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 4. Carry
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 4. Carry
4. Carry

**Thesis:** earn a yield/roll premium for holding a position.

| Carry type | Example | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| **Futures roll** | Long futures in contango/backwardation | Roll cost, spot shock |
| **Dividend capture** | Buy before ex-date, sell after | Price drop, tax, execution |
| **Currency carry** | High-yield vs low-yield currency | FX crash, funding squeeze |
| **Options carry** | Short premium/theta | Gap, vol spike |

**Rule:** carry strategies earn small amounts repeatedly and can lose a lot in a
tail event. Size for the tail, not the average.

---

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 5. Hedging
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 5. Hedging
5. Hedging

**Thesis:** reduce unwanted risk, not maximize return.

| Hedge | What it does | Cost/risk |
|---|---|---|
| **Beta hedge** | Short index futures vs long portfolio | Basis risk, margin |
| **Protective put** | Buy downside insurance | Premium drag |
| **Collar** | Buy put, sell call | Capped upside |
| **Covered call** | Sell call against holdings | Capped upside, assignment |
| **Cross-asset** | Gold/USD/rates hedge | Correlation instability |

**Hedging is a cost centre.** Its job is to keep you in the game, not to make you rich.
Measure hedge cost as a % of portfolio per year.

---

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 6. Quant / systematic
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 6. Quant / systematic
6. Quant / systematic

**Thesis:** a repeatable statistical edge can be executed mechanically.

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 6. Quant / systematic > Pipeline
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 6. Quant / systematic > Pipeline
Pipeline

```
Hypothesis → Data → Signal → Backtest → Costs → Robustness → Paper → Live → Monitor
```

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 6. Quant / systematic > What makes it valid
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 6. Quant / systematic > What makes it valid
What makes it valid

1. **Economic rationale:** why should the edge exist?
2. **Clean data:** survivorship, look-ahead, corporate actions, timestamps.
3. **Realistic costs:** brokerage, STT, slippage, impact.
4. **Out-of-sample:** train/test/walk-forward.
5. **Parameter stability:** small changes should not destroy results.
6. **Capacity:** can you execute the size?
7. **Monitoring:** kill switch, drawdown limits, drift detection.

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 6. Quant / systematic > India-specific
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 6. Quant / systematic > India-specific
India-specific

- SEBI algo rules: broker/exchange approval, audit trail, risk controls; use the current
  circular.
- Retail algo via broker APIs is allowed within the framework; "black box" promises
  are a red flag.
- F&O margins, lot sizes and expiry rules change; backtest with current costs.
- Data quality is the biggest hidden risk.

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 6. Quant / systematic > Failure modes
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 6. Quant / systematic > Failure modes
Failure modes

- Overfitting (too many parameters, too few trades).
- Look-ahead bias.
- Survivorship bias.
- Ignoring costs/slippage.
- Regime shift.
- Leverage on a fragile model.

---

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 7. Comparison
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 7. Comparison
7. Comparison

| Style | Edge | Capital need | Skill | Main risk | Retail fit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Event | Information | Medium | High | Gap/interpretation | Good for experienced |
| Arbitrage | Convergence | High | High | Execution/crowding | Low–medium |
| Market making | Spread/speed | Very high | Very high | Adverse selection | Poor |
| Carry | Yield/roll | Medium | Medium | Tail event | Selective |
| Hedging | Risk reduction | Medium | Medium | Cost/basis | Good |
| Quant | Statistical | Medium | High | Overfit/regime | Good for coders |

---

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 8. Exercises
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > 8. Exercises
8. Exercises

1. Take one recent event (earnings/RBI/budget) and write the event study checklist.
2. Compute the cash-futures basis for one index and explain why it exists.
3. Compare a protective put vs a collar on the same portfolio.
4. Write a quant hypothesis with an economic rationale.
5. List five costs your backtest must include.
6. Explain why market making is not a retail strategy.

---

chunks.title: 04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > Teluglish takeaway
chunks.text:
04 — Event, Arbitrage, Quant & Institutional Styles > Teluglish takeaway
Teluglish takeaway

Event trading lo **"good news = bullish"** anedi rule kadu; expectations and positioning
chudandi.
Arbitrage lo spread kanipisthe, meeru miss avutunna risk emito adagandi.
Market making/HFT retail game kadu; latency/infrastructure war.
Quant lo **overfit** = backtest beautiful, live disaster. Costs + out-of-sample lekapote
nammakandi.

chunks.title: 05 — Options Trading Styles
chunks.text:
05 — Options Trading Styles
05 — Options Trading Styles

**Holding period:** hours to weeks
**Edge:** direction, volatility, time decay, hedging
**Risk:** high to very high
**India fit:** experienced traders with Greeks, margin and assignment knowledge

> Options are not "cheap futures". They are a **different asset class** with three
> dimensions: direction, volatility and time. Most retail option losses come from
> ignoring two of the three.

---

chunks.title: 05 — Options Trading Styles > 1. The three dimensions
chunks.text:
05 — Options Trading Styles > 1. The three dimensions
1. The three dimensions

| Dimension | Driver | Greek | What can hurt you |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Direction** | Spot move | Delta | Being wrong on the market |
| **Volatility** | Implied volatility | Vega | IV crush after an event |
| **Time** | Days to expiry | Theta | Premium decays even if direction is right |

Before any option trade, answer:

1. What is my **directional view**?
2. Is implied volatility **high or low** vs history?
3. How many **days** does the thesis need?
4. What is my **max loss** and margin?
5. What happens if the event is a **non-event**?

---

chunks.title: 05 — Options Trading Styles > 2. Directional options
chunks.text:
05 — Options Trading Styles > 2. Directional options
2. Directional options

| Strategy | View | Max loss | Max profit | Best when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Long call** | Bullish | Premium | Unlimited | IV low, enough time |
| **Long put** | Bearish | Premium | High | IV low, downside hedge |
| **Bull call spread** | Moderately bullish | Net debit | Capped | IV high, target known |
| **Bear put spread** | Moderately bearish | Net debit | Capped | IV high, target known |
| **Risk reversal** | Bullish/bearish with hedge | Varies | Varies | Strong view, cost control |

**Long options:** you pay theta and vega. A correct direction with IV crush can still
lose money.

**Debit spreads:** reduce cost and vega, but cap profit. Better for defined-risk
traders.

---

chunks.title: 05 — Options Trading Styles > 3. Income / non-directional options
chunks.text:
05 — Options Trading Styles > 3. Income / non-directional options
3. Income / non-directional options

| Strategy | View | Max loss | Works when | Fails when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Covered call** | Neutral/mildly bullish | Stock downside | Range, high IV | Sharp rally (capped) |
| **Cash-secured put** | Neutral/mildly bullish | Strike − premium | Range, high IV | Sharp fall |
| **Iron condor** | Range | Width − credit | Low volatility, range | Breakout/vol spike |
| **Short strangle** | Range | Large/naked | High IV, range | Gap/trend |
| **Short straddle** | Range | Large/naked | High IV, pin | Big move |
| **Long straddle** | Big move expected | Premium | Event, high vol | IV crush, range |
| **Long strangle** | Big move, cheaper | Premium | Event, high vol | IV crush, range |
| **Butterfly** | Pin at strike | Net debit | Range, expiry | Big move |
| **Calendar** | Time/vol differential | Net debit | Low near-term vol | Vol spike, trend |

**Short premium** has a dangerous payoff: small gains repeatedly, large loss in a gap.
Size by **max loss**, not by credit received.

---

chunks.title: 05 — Options Trading Styles > 4. Event-vol trading
chunks.text:
05 — Options Trading Styles > 4. Event-vol trading
4. Event-vol trading

Events create a **volatility cycle**:

```
Pre-event: IV rises → event: IV peaks → post-event: IV crush → theta dominates
```

Examples: earnings, RBI policy, budget, election results, war headlines, index
rebalancing.

**Checklist:**

- What is the **expected move** (straddle price/IV)?
- Is the event **binary** or gradual?
- Is IV **high or low** vs its own history?
- Can I exit before the event?
- What is the **post-event drift** hypothesis?
- What happens if the event is delayed/cancelled?

**Mistake:** buying options right before earnings because "it will move". The move may
happen, but IV crush can still produce a loss.

---

chunks.title: 05 — Options Trading Styles > 5. Hedging styles
chunks.text:
05 — Options Trading Styles > 5. Hedging styles
5. Hedging styles

| Hedge | Protection | Cost | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Protective put** | Downside below strike | Premium | Portfolio insurance |
| **Collar** | Downside + capped upside | Low/zero net cost | Concentrated holdings |
| **Covered call** | Small downside cushion | Capped upside | Income on holdings |
| **Put spread** | Downside to a limit | Lower cost | Budget hedge |
| **Index futures short** | Beta hedge | Margin, basis | Portfolio beta control |

**Hedge sizing:** notional coverage, delta coverage, cost as % of portfolio, and the
scenario where the hedge fails (gap, correlation break).

---

chunks.title: 05 — Options Trading Styles > 6. India-specific rules
chunks.text:
05 — Options Trading Styles > 6. India-specific rules
6. India-specific rules

| Item | What to know |
|---|---|
| **Index options** | European, cash-settled |
| **Stock options** | European, physically settled |
| **Weekly expiry** | Only select index contracts; use current schedule |
| **Lot size** | Exchange-defined; minimum contract size rules tightened in 2024–25 |
| **Margin** | SPAN + exposure; short options need margin |
| **STT** | 0.1% on sell premium (current rate) |
| **Upfront premium** | Buyer pays premium upfront; no carry |
| **Intraday monitoring** | SEBI tightened position monitoring |
| **Assignment** | Stock options can result in delivery obligations |
| **Liquidity** | Far OTM strikes can have wide spreads |

> Use current lot sizes, expiry, margin and STT from NSE/BSE/SEBI; rules change.

---

chunks.title: 05 — Options Trading Styles > 7. Risk rules for options
chunks.text:
05 — Options Trading Styles > 7. Risk rules for options
7. Risk rules for options

| Rule | Default |
|---|---|
| Max loss per trade | 0.5–1% of capital |
| Max open option risk | 3–6% |
| Naked short options | Avoid for retail |
| Position size | Based on **max loss**, not premium |
| Expiry | Avoid holding near-expiry gamma unless intentional |
| Event | Reduce size or use defined-risk spreads |
| Liquidity | Trade tight spreads; check depth |
| Assignment | Know physical settlement obligations |

**Example:** ₹5,00,000 capital, 1% max loss = ₹5,000. A spread costing ₹8 with lot size
50 has max loss ₹400 per lot → 12 lots max (₹4,800), before costs. A naked short
strangle may have a much larger theoretical max loss — do not size it on credit.

---

chunks.title: 05 — Options Trading Styles > 8. Common mistakes
chunks.text:
05 — Options Trading Styles > 8. Common mistakes
8. Common mistakes

- Buying far OTM options because they are "cheap".
- Ignoring IV crush.
- Selling naked options for premium.
- Holding stock options into expiry without delivery funds.
- Using options as a lottery ticket.
- Averaging down a losing option position.
- Trading illiquid strikes.
- No max-loss calculation.

---

chunks.title: 05 — Options Trading Styles > 9. Exercises
chunks.text:
05 — Options Trading Styles > 9. Exercises
9. Exercises

1. Draw payoff diagrams for long call, bull call spread, iron condor, covered call.
2. Calculate the expected move from a straddle price.
3. Compare IV before and after an earnings event.
4. Build a defined-risk hedge for a ₹5 lakh portfolio.

chunks.title: 05 — Options Trading Styles > Teluglish takeaway
chunks.text:
05 — Options Trading Styles > Teluglish takeaway
Teluglish takeaway

Options lo **direction, volatility, time** — moodu dimensions; spot price okkate chudakandi.
Event mundu IV high untundi; event tarvata **IV crush** valla option loser avvachu.
Naked short options = small profits, big tail risk; retail ki **defined-risk spreads** best.
Max loss batti size cheyandi, premium batti kadu. Expiry/assignment rules verify cheyandi.

chunks.title: 06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework)
chunks.text:
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework)
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework)

**Goal:** pick one primary style and one backup — not all of them.
**Rule:** the best style is the one you can execute **consistently**, **afford**, and
**survive** emotionally and financially.

> A style you cannot execute is not a style. It is a fantasy with a spreadsheet.

---

chunks.title: 06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 1. The six filters
chunks.text:
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 1. The six filters
1. The six filters

| Filter | Question | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Time** | How many uninterrupted hours/day? | Scalping/intraday need screen time |
| **Capital** | How much can you lose without life impact? | F&O needs margin; small accounts are fragile |
| **Temperament** | Fast decisions or patient waiting? | Style must fit your psychology |
| **Skill** | Can you read structure, size, journal? | Complexity must match competence |
| **Cost** | Does the edge survive costs? | High-frequency styles are cost-sensitive |
| **Risk capacity** | Can you survive a 20–30% drawdown? | Leverage can force exits |

---

chunks.title: 06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 2. Decision tree
chunks.text:
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 2. Decision tree
2. Decision tree

```
START
│
├─ Can you watch markets 4–6+ hours/day?
│   ├─ YES → Do you have a tested intraday edge and low costs?
│   │         ├─ YES → Intraday (small size) or scalping (only if automated)
│   │         └─ NO  → Swing with intraday timing
│   └─ NO  → Can you check once/twice a day?
│             ├─ YES → Swing or positional
│             └─ NO  → Investment / ETF / SIP
│
├─ Is capital < ₹1 lakh?
│   ├─ YES → Delivery/ETF/swing; avoid naked F&O
│   └─ NO  → Continue
│
├─ Do you have options/Greeks knowledge?
│   ├─ YES → Defined-risk options (spreads/hedges)
│   └─ NO  → Equity/futures first
│
└─ Are you emotional after losses?
    ├─ YES → Rules-based swing/positional, smaller size
    └─ NO  → Any style, with risk limits
```

---

chunks.title: 06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 3. Time tiers
chunks.text:
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 3. Time tiers
3. Time tiers

| Time/day | Realistic styles | Not realistic |
|---|---|---|
| **< 30 min** | Positional, investment, ETF/SIP | Scalping, intraday |
| **1–2 hours** | Swing, positional | Full-time intraday |
| **3–4 hours** | Intraday (selective), swing | High-frequency scalping |
| **5–8+ hours** | Intraday, scalping, quant | — |

**Important:** "Time available" means **uninterrupted**, not "phone in pocket". If you
are in meetings, you cannot manage an intraday stop.

---

chunks.title: 06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 4. Capital tiers
chunks.text:
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 4. Capital tiers
4. Capital tiers

| Capital | Realistic focus | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| **< ₹50,000** | ETF/SIP, delivery, paper trading | Futures/options, leveraged intraday |
| **₹50k–₹1 lakh** | Delivery/swing, small ETF | Naked options, over-leverage |
| **₹1–5 lakh** | Swing + defined-risk options | Concentration, high-frequency |
| **₹5–10 lakh** | Diversified swing, spreads, hedges | Naked short options |
| **₹10 lakh+** | Multi-style, portfolio risk | Ego, over-trading |

**Rule:** never risk more than **1% per trade**; for a small account, 0.25–0.5% is
better because fixed costs are a larger percentage.

---

chunks.title: 06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 5. Temperament
chunks.text:
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 5. Temperament
5. Temperament

| Temperament | Better styles | Worse styles |
|---|---|---|
| **Patient, analytical** | Positional, trend, value overlay | Scalping |
| **Fast, decisive** | Intraday, momentum | Slow positional |
| **Anxious, loss-averse** | Swing with small size, ETF | Naked options, leverage |
| **Competitive, action-seeking** | Intraday with strict limits | Revenge trading |
| **Systematic, detail-oriented** | Quant, rule-based swing | Discretionary news |
| **Narrative-driven** | Event/positional with research | Mean reversion without rules |

No temperament is "wrong". The wrong choice is forcing a style that fights it.

---

chunks.title: 06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 6. Skill tiers
chunks.text:
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 6. Skill tiers
6. Skill tiers

| Skill level | What you can do | Next step |
|---|---|---|
| **Beginner** | Order types, S/R, basic risk | Paper swing, 30 trades |
| **Intermediate** | Setup definition, backtest, journal | Small live swing, 100 trades |
| **Advanced** | Derivatives, Greeks, systematic | Defined-risk options, quant |
| **Pro** | Portfolio risk, execution, review | Multi-style, capacity |

Do not skip levels because a strategy looks simple. Execution is the hard part.

---

chunks.title: 06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 7. Style scorecard (10 questions)
chunks.text:
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 7. Style scorecard (10 questions)
7. Style scorecard (10 questions)

Score each 1–5 (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree).

| # | Question | Score |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | I have the uninterrupted time this style requires. | |
| 2 | I can afford the maximum loss without changing my life. | |
| 3 | I understand the edge and can explain it in one sentence. | |
| 4 | I can execute the entry/exit without hesitation. | |
| 5 | I can hold through normal volatility without panic. | |
| 6 | I have backtested/paper-traded at least 30 trades. | |
| 7 | I know the costs and they are < 1/3 of my target. | |
| 8 | I can journal and review every trade. | |
| 9 | The style fits my temperament. | |
| 10 | I have a risk policy and a kill switch. | |

**Interpretation:**

- **40–50:** good fit; paper trade 30 more, then small live.
- **30–39:** conditional; fix the weak items first.
- **20–29:** poor fit; choose a simpler style.
- **< 20:** do not trade this style with real money.

---

chunks.title: 06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 8. 30/60/90-day plan > Days 1–30 — Learn and observe
chunks.text:
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 8. 30/60/90-day plan > Days 1–30 — Learn and observe
Days 1–30 — Learn and observe

- Read this module + relevant specialist module.
- Pick one style.
- Journal 20 paper trades.
- Track costs, slippage and rule adherence.
- No live money.

chunks.title: 06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 8. 30/60/90-day plan > Days 31–60 — Paper to micro live
chunks.text:
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 8. 30/60/90-day plan > Days 31–60 — Paper to micro live
Days 31–60 — Paper to micro live

- 10–20 paper trades with a written plan.
- If expectancy > 0 after costs, start micro live at 0.25% risk.
- Max 2 trades/day; no revenge.
- Weekly review.

chunks.title: 06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 8. 30/60/90-day plan > Days 61–90 — Evaluate
chunks.text:
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 8. 30/60/90-day plan > Days 61–90 — Evaluate
Days 61–90 — Evaluate

- 30+ paper/micro trades.
- Metrics: expectancy, win rate, payoff, max DD, cost %, rule adherence.
- If positive and disciplined, increase to 0.5–1% risk.
- If negative, fix the process or change style — do not increase size.

---

chunks.title: 06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 9. Style switching rules
chunks.text:
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 9. Style switching rules
9. Style switching rules

Switch only if **all three** are true:

1. You have **100+ trades** of data in the current style.
2. The failure is **structural** (no edge after costs), not a normal drawdown.
3. You have a written hypothesis for why the new style fits better.

Do not switch after:

- 3 losses in a row.
- A big win (overconfidence).
- A YouTube video.
- Someone else's P&L screenshot.
- A market regime change without testing.

---

chunks.title: 06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 10. Red flags
chunks.text:
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 10. Red flags
10. Red flags

- You need daily income from trading.
- You are using borrowed money/EMI/credit.
- You cannot explain max loss.
- You have no written plan.
- You check P&L every few minutes.
- You increase size after a loss.
- You trade illiquid instruments.
- You follow tips/copy trading without a thesis.
- You have not journaled 30 trades.
- You think a style is "guaranteed".

---

chunks.title: 06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 11. Exercises
chunks.text:
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > 11. Exercises
11. Exercises

1. Complete the scorecard for two styles.
2. Write a one-page "why this style fits me" note.
3. Calculate your monthly cost budget for the style.
4. Define your max drawdown and kill switch.
5. Build a 30/60/90-day calendar.
6. Ask a friend to challenge your style choice.

---

chunks.title: 06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > Teluglish takeaway
chunks.text:
06 — Choose Your Style (Decision Framework) > Teluglish takeaway
Teluglish takeaway

Style selection lo **time, capital, temperament, skill, cost, risk capacity** — six
filters.
Job unte swing/positional; full-time unte intraday; small capital unte F&O avoid.
Scorecard lo 30 kante takkuva unte, aa style ki real money vaddu.
Style switch cheyali ante **100+ trades data** undali; 3 losses ki kadu.

chunks.title: 07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style
chunks.text:
07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style
07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style

**Goal:** the same risk discipline, adapted to each style's failure mode.
**Rule:** risk is defined before entry, not after the loss.

> Every style has a different way of hurting you:
> intraday hurts through leverage, swing through gaps, options through time,
> quant through overfitting, and scalping through costs.

---

chunks.title: 07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > 1. Risk per style
chunks.text:
07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > 1. Risk per style
1. Risk per style

| Style | Max risk/trade | Max daily loss | Max open risk | Stop type | Key risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Scalping** | 0.25–0.5% | 1% | 2% | Hard + time | Costs, slippage |
| **Intraday** | 0.5–1% | 2% | 3% | Hard + time | Leverage, overtrading |
| **Swing** | 0.5–1% | 3% | 3–6% | Structure/ATR | Overnight gap |
| **Positional** | 0.5–1.5% | 4% | 6–10% | Thesis/ATR | Event/fundamental |
| **Trend** | 0.5–1% | 3% | 6% | ATR/trailing | Whipsaw |
| **Momentum** | 0.5–1% | 3% | 6% | Rank drop/stop | Reversal/crowding |
| **Mean reversion** | 0.5–1% | 3% | 4% | Support/ATR | Falling knife |
| **Event** | 0.25–0.5% | 2% | 2–4% | Event invalidation | Gap/interpretation |
| **Options** | 0.5–1% max loss | 2% | 3–6% | Max loss/premium | IV crush, assignment |
| **Arbitrage** | 0.25–0.5% | 1% | 2% | Spread stop | Execution/crowding |
| **Quant** | 0.5–1% | Portfolio vol | Portfolio limit | Model stop | Overfit/regime |
| **Hedging** | Cost budget | — | — | Hedge ratio | Basis/correlation |

**Note:** these are baseline defaults; calibrate to your capital and drawdown tolerance.

---

chunks.title: 07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > 2. Stop placement by style
chunks.text:
07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > 2. Stop placement by style
2. Stop placement by style

| Style | Stop logic | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Scalping | Fixed ticks/ATR + time stop | Mental stops |
| Intraday | Structure/ATR + time stop | Widening after entry |
| Swing | Swing low/high, ATR, invalidation level | Stop inside noise |
| Positional | Thesis invalidation + ATR | Stop based on "conviction" |
| Trend | 1.5–3× ATR or trailing | Moving stop away |
| Mean reversion | Beyond support/resistance | Averaging down |
| Event | Event thesis invalidated | Holding through binary risk |
| Options | Max loss/premium/underlying level | Hoping for expiry |
| Quant | Model stop + drawdown limit | Discretionary override |

**Gap risk:** a stop is not a guarantee. Size so that a gap through the stop is still
survivable.

---

chunks.title: 07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > 3. Position sizing examples > Equity swing
chunks.text:
07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > 3. Position sizing examples > Equity swing
Equity swing

₹5,00,000 capital, 1% risk = ₹5,000.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Entry | ₹250 |
| Stop | ₹235 |
| Risk/unit | ₹15 |
| Quantity | 333 shares |
| Position | ₹83,250 |
| Gap scenario: price opens ₹225 | Loss ≈ ₹8,325 (1.67%) |

If that gap loss is unacceptable, reduce quantity.

chunks.title: 07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > 3. Position sizing examples > Options
chunks.text:
07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > 3. Position sizing examples > Options
Options

₹5,00,000 capital, 1% max loss = ₹5,000.

- A debit spread costs ₹8, lot size 50 → max loss ₹400/lot.
- Max lots = ₹5,000 / ₹400 = 12 lots.
- Costs reduce this to 11 lots.

Never size short options by the credit received; size by max loss/margin.

---

chunks.title: 07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > 4. Psychology by style
chunks.text:
07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > 4. Psychology by style
4. Psychology by style

| Style | Emotional trap | Countermeasure |
|---|---|---|
| **Scalping** | Impulse, overtrading | Fixed trade count, timer, hard stop |
| **Intraday** | Revenge after loss | Daily loss limit, two-loss stop |
| **Swing** | Checking every hour, fear of gap | Once-a-day review, event plan |
| **Positional** | Boredom, thesis creep | Written thesis + review dates |
| **Trend** | Cutting winners early | Trailing rules, R-multiple targets |
| **Momentum** | Chasing extended leaders | Rank/valuation filter, staged entry |
| **Mean reversion** | Catching falling knives | Regime filter, hard stop |
| **Breakout** | Chasing false breaks | Wait for close/retest |
| **Event** | Confusing outcome with process | Grade decision, not P&L |
| **Options** | Hope at expiry | Max loss, pre-defined exit |
| **Quant** | Overfitting/overconfidence | OOS, walk-forward, paper |
| **Arbitrage** | Assuming "risk-free" | Stress test execution/crowding |

**Tilt warning signs:** checking P&L constantly, widening stops, increasing size after
loss, "one more trade", blaming the market.

**Tilt protocol:** stop → close platform → 30–60 min break → write what happened →
no re-entry today → review tomorrow.

---

chunks.title: 07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > 5. Journal KPIs by style
chunks.text:
07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > 5. Journal KPIs by style
5. Journal KPIs by style

| Style | Must-track metrics |
|---|---|
| **Scalping** | Cost/trade, slippage, trades/day, avg R, rule adherence |
| **Intraday** | MFE/MAE, time-of-day P&L, overtrading count, daily loss |
| **Swing** | Overnight gap P&L, holding days, event exposure, hit rate |
| **Positional** | Thesis validation, earnings surprises, regime tags |
| **Trend** | Win rate, avg win/loss R, max DD, whipsaw count |
| **Momentum** | Turnover, rank decay, sector exposure, factor drawdown |
| **Mean reversion** | Time-to-mean, stop hits, regime, falling-knife count |
| **Event** | Surprise vs priced-in, gap, post-event drift, IV change |
| **Options** | Delta/theta/vega P&L, IV entry/exit, assignment, max loss |
| **Quant** | Sharpe, Sortino, max DD, turnover, OOS decay, capacity |
| **Arbitrage** | Spread capture, fill rate, borrow/margin cost, crowding |

**Universal metrics:** expectancy (R), profit factor, win rate, payoff ratio, max
drawdown, cost as % of gross profit, rule adherence grade.

---

chunks.title: 07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > 6. The 100-trade plan
chunks.text:
07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > 6. The 100-trade plan
6. The 100-trade plan

| Phase | Trades | Size | Goal |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Paper** | 30 | Zero | Learn the process, not P&L |
| **2. Micro live** | 30 | 0.25–0.5% risk | Test execution/slippage |
| **3. Scale** | 40 | 0.5–1% risk | Test consistency |
| **Review** | — | — | Decide: continue, fix, or stop |

**Continue only if:**

- Positive expectancy after costs.
- Max drawdown within plan.
- Rule adherence ≥ 90%.
- No revenge/oversized trades.
- Process is repeatable without adrenaline.

**Stop and review if:**

- Max drawdown hits 10–15%.
- Three rule breaks in a week.
- You cannot sleep.
- You are trading to recover losses.

---

chunks.text:
07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > 7. Common mistakes by style

| Scalping | Ignoring costs, overtrading |
| Intraday | No stop, revenge, leverage |

chunks.title: 07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > Teluglish takeaway
chunks.text:
07 — Risk, Psychology & Journal by Style > Teluglish takeaway
Teluglish takeaway

Style marithe risk rules marutayi, kani **risk per trade 0.5–1%** anedi base.
Scalping lo cost, swing lo gap, options lo time, quant lo overfit — ee failure modes
munnu chudandi.
Journal lo P&L kadu — **process grade, slippage, rule adherence** track cheyandi.
100 trades tarvata ne scale; drawdown 10–15% hit aithe size half cheyandi.

08 — Case Studies & Workbook

chunks.title: 08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 1 — 2024 election shock (4 June 2024)
chunks.text:
08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 1 — 2024 election shock (4 June 2024)
Case study 1 — 2024 election shock (4 June 2024)

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Event** | Lok Sabha results; BJP won 240 seats, NDA reached 293; exit polls had predicted a bigger BJP majority |
| **Market** | Sensex fell ~4,390 points (−5.7%) to 72,079; Nifty fell ~5.9% to 21,884 |
| **Regime** | Strong uptrend into the event; high expectations; low hedging |
| **Recovery** | New highs within weeks as policy continuity was priced |

**Style lens:**

| Style | What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Intraday** | Gap-down, volatility spike, stop slippage | Event gaps can exceed stops |
| **Swing** | Forced to sit through a 5–6% gap | Event calendar must be part of the plan |
| **Positional** | Thesis intact if policy continuity; drawdown temporary | Separate political noise from earnings |
| **Options** | IV spike, put/call chaos; early exit mattered | Event vol is two-sided |

**Lesson:** a known event is not a known outcome. Size for the gap, not the exit poll.

---

chunks.title: 08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 2 — 2025 tariff shock ("Liberation Day")
chunks.text:
08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 2 — 2025 tariff shock ("Liberation Day")
Case study 2 — 2025 tariff shock ("Liberation Day")

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Event** | US announced sweeping tariffs on 2 April 2025; global risk-off |
| **Market** | S&P ~−19% peak-to-trough; India exposed through exports, rupee and sentiment |
| **India** | US–India tensions; 50% tariffs on many Indian goods effective 27 August 2025 |
| **Recovery** | S&P reclaimed highs by late June 2025; India negotiated, and the US later reduced tariffs to 18% in February 2026 |

**Style lens:**

| Style | What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Trend** | Trend broke; trailing stops saved capital | Regime change > prediction |
| **Event** | Headline-driven whipsaw; policy reversal possible | Trade the path, not the first headline |
| **Swing** | Exporters/rupee hit; domestic demand cushioned | Sector selection mattered |
| **Options** | IV spike; naked short premium dangerous | Tail risk is real |

**Lesson:** policy shocks can reverse. A tariff is a **negotiation**, not a permanent
regime — but the market can fall a lot before the reversal.

---

chunks.title: 08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 3 — 2025 India–Pakistan conflict
chunks.text:
08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 3 — 2025 India–Pakistan conflict
Case study 3 — 2025 India–Pakistan conflict

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Event** | Pahalgam attack 22 April 2025; Operation Sindoor 7 May; ceasefire 10 May |
| **Market** | Brief risk-off; defense stocks rallied; oil/rupee watched |
| **Regime** | Geopolitical shock inside a tariff-driven correction |

**Style lens:**

| Style | What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Event** | Defense rally; quick de-escalation | Short war = short shock |
| **Intraday** | Headline gaps; stops slipped | War headlines are not intraday setups |
| **Positional** | Thesis unchanged unless oil/fiscal regime changed | Separate security from macro |
| **Hedging** | Gold/puts/defense hedge worked short-term | Hedge cost vs duration |

**Lesson:** regional wars are usually a **trade**, not a regime change — unless they hit
oil, shipping or fiscal credibility.

chunks.title: 08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 4 — 2026 Iran war and oil shock
chunks.text:
08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 4 — 2026 Iran war and oil shock
Case study 4 — 2026 Iran war and oil shock

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Event** | US–Israel–Iran war began 28 February 2026; Khamenei assassinated; Strait of Hormuz blocked |
| **Market** | S&P bottom 6,316.91 on 30 March 2026; +17.3% to 7,411.98 by 24 July 2026 |
| **Oil** | Brent peak ~$118; later volatile (~$71–$100 range) |
| **Ceasefire** | Initial 8 April; collapsed 8 July; fragile |
| **India** | Crude/LPG inflation, rupee pressure; RBI later hawkish (Oct 2026) |

**Style lens:**

| Style | What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Event** | Oil/inflation shock; headline whipsaw | War is an inflation shock first |
| **Trend** | Recovery trend after April, but fragile | Partial V, not clean V |
| **Positional** | Energy/defense/import-substitution themes | Macro transmission matters |
| **Options** | IV spike and crush; gap risk | Defined risk > naked premium |

**Lesson:** do not assume the April low was the final low. A war/oil shock can create a
**fragile recovery**, not a clean V.

---

chunks.title: 08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 5 — 2020 COVID crash
chunks.text:
08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 5 — 2020 COVID crash
Case study 5 — 2020 COVID crash

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Event** | Global pandemic; lockdowns from March 2020 |
| **Market** | S&P −34% in 33 days (bottom 23 March 2020); Sensex −38.5% |
| **Policy** | Rate cuts, liquidity, fiscal support |
| **Recovery** | V-shaped globally; India reclaimed peak in ~10 months |

**Style lens:**

| Style | What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Trend** | Fast crash, fast recovery; whipsaw | Policy response can truncate the cycle |
| **Mean reversion** | Panic rebound worked after washout | Regime filter + size |
| **Positional** | Long-term thesis intact; drawdown painful | Liquidity > opinion |
| **Options** | Long puts/vol spike; then IV crush | Exit plan matters |

**Lesson:** the **policy response** is part of the thesis. Fast, massive support can
create a V; slow support can create a U/L.

chunks.title: 08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 6 — 2008 Global Financial Crisis
chunks.text:
08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 6 — 2008 Global Financial Crisis
Case study 6 — 2008 Global Financial Crisis

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Event** | US housing/credit crisis; Lehman collapse September 2008 |
| **Market** | S&P −57%; Sensex −61% |
| **Recovery** | S&P reclaimed peak ~2013; Sensex ~2014 |
| **Policy** | Bailouts, rate cuts, QE |

**Style lens:**

| Style | What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Trend** | Strong downtrend; trend following/hedging worked | Trend can be your friend in a crisis |
| **Long-only** | Deep drawdown; recovery took years | Leverage can force exit at the bottom |
| **Mean reversion** | Catching falling knives failed repeatedly | Credit crises are not normal mean reversion |
| **Options** | Puts/vol hedge paid; short premium blew up | Tail risk is the whole game |

**Lesson:** in a **credit crisis**, the recovery depends on deleveraging and policy, not
on a chart pattern.

chunks.title: 08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 7 — 1992 Harshad Mehta scam
chunks.text:
08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 7 — 1992 Harshad Mehta scam
Case study 7 — 1992 Harshad Mehta scam

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Event** | Bank receipts/fake securities; liquidity-driven boom; scam exposed |
| **Market** | Sensex fell 12.77% on 28 April 1992; roughly halved over the following year |
| **Regulatory** | SEBI got statutory powers in 1992; market reforms followed |

**Style lens:**

| Style | What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Event** | Liquidity/trust shock; broad sell-off | Scams are liquidity events |
| **Trend** | Boom/bust; trend reversal | Leverage unwinds fast |
| **Positional** | Quality survived; leveraged names did not | Governance is a risk factor |
| **Options** | Not a major retail market then | Instruments change, anatomy doesn't |

**Lesson:** when the **plumbing** (settlement, bank receipts, liquidity) is questioned,
the whole market re-rates. Governance is not a footnote.

chunks.title: 08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 8 — 2026 NSE IPO
chunks.text:
08 — Case Studies & Workbook > Case study 8 — 2026 NSE IPO
Case study 8 — 2026 NSE IPO

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Event** | NSE listed on BSE on 24 September 2026 |
| **Size** | IPO ~₹22,569 crore; 5.71x oversubscribed |
| **Context** | One of India's largest IPOs; exchange listing its own shares |
| **Market** | Event/IPO flows; valuation debate |

| Style | What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Event/IPO** | Subscription/listing flows | IPO is an event, not a style |
| **Swing** | Listing pop/fade; lock-in/float | Supply/demand matters |
| **Positional** | Business quality/valuation, not listing day | Wait for price discovery |
| **Options** | Not immediately relevant | Don't force a strategy |

**Lesson:** an IPO is a **liquidity event**. The listing pop is not an investment thesis.

chunks.title: 🧭 Module 14 — Trading Types: The Complete Style Playbook > Why this module exists
chunks.text:
🧭 Module 14 — Trading Types: The Complete Style Playbook > Why this module exists
Why this module exists

Most traders fail not because their chart pattern was wrong, but because they chose
a style that did not fit their life.

- A job-going person tries scalping at 9:15 a.m. and blows up on costs and distractions.
- A patient investor tries 5-minute charts and overtrades.
- A small account tries naked options and one gap wipes out months of gains.
- A systematic thinker keeps switching styles after three losses.

This module gives you the **complete map** — every major trading type, how it makes
money, what it costs, when it fails, and who it suits.

---

chunks.title: 🧭 Module 14 — Trading Types: The Complete Style Playbook > The six lenses
chunks.text:
🧭 Module 14 — Trading Types: The Complete Style Playbook > The six lenses
The six lenses

Every trading type can be described from six angles. Do not mix them up.

| Lens | Question | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Holding period** | How long is the trade open? | Scalp, intraday, swing, positional, investment |
| **Edge/style** | Why should it work? | Trend, momentum, mean reversion, breakout, event, arbitrage |
| **Instrument** | What are you trading? | Delivery equity, intraday equity, futures, options, ETF |
| **Execution** | How is it run? | Discretionary, systematic, algo, hybrid |
| **Direction** | What is the exposure? | Long-only, long-short, market-neutral, hedged |
| **Risk mode** | How is risk controlled? | Directional, hedged, arbitrage, portfolio insurance |

A single trade has **one value on each lens**. Example:

```
Buy Nifty futures at 9:20, sell at 11:00
Holding: intraday · Edge: momentum · Instrument: futures
Execution: discretionary · Direction: long · Risk: directional
```

---

chunks.text:
🧭 Module 14 — Trading Types: The Complete Style Playbook > One-page taxonomy
One-page taxonomy

| Type | Holding | Main edge | Cost sensitivity | Risk | Typical user |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Scalping** | Seconds–minutes | Spread, order flow, speed | Extreme | Very high | Full-time / algo |
| **Intraday** | Same day | Momentum, VWAP, levels | High | High | Active trader |
| **Swing** | 2–10 days | Trend, pullback, breakout | Medium | Medium | Job-going trader |
| **Positional** | Weeks–months | Trend + catalyst | Low–medium | Medium | Patient trader |
| **Investment** | Years | Earnings, quality, compounding | Low | Low–medium | Long-term investor |
| **Trend following** | Weeks–months | Persistence of trend | Low | Medium | Rules-based trader |
| **Momentum** | Weeks–months | Relative strength | Medium | Medium–high | Rotation trader |
| **Mean reversion** | Days–weeks | Overreaction | Medium | Medium–high | Range trader |
| **Breakout** | Days–weeks | Volatility expansion | Medium | Medium–high | Active trader |
| **Event/news** | Hours–weeks | Information surprise | High | High | Event specialist |
| **Arbitrage** | Seconds–days | Price inefficiency | Low per trade | Low–medium | Institutional / quant |
| **Quant/systematic** | Varies | Statistical edge | Medium | Medium | Coder / analyst |
| **Options income** | Weeks | Theta / implied volatility | Medium–high | High | Options trader |
| **Hedging** | Varies | Risk reduction | Medium | Low (cost drag) | Portfolio owner |

**Also covered in the files:** pullback, market making/HFT, and carry.

chunks.title: 🧭 Module 14 — Trading Types: The Complete Style Playbook > How to use this module
chunks.text:
🧭 Module 14 — Trading Types: The Complete Style Playbook > How to use this module
How to use this module

1. **Read the taxonomy** and classify 10 of your past trades.
2. **Pick two styles** that fit your time and capital.
3. **Paper trade one style** for 30 trades.
4. **Backtest 100+ trades** with costs and slippage.
5. **Write a one-page playbook** for the chosen style.
6. **Review** after 30, 60 and 90 days.

Do not try to learn every style at once. Pick one primary style and one backup.

---

chunks.title: 🧭 Module 14 — Trading Types: The Complete Style Playbook > The 6-question style test
chunks.text:
🧭 Module 14 — Trading Types: The Complete Style Playbook > The 6-question style test
The 6-question style test

Answer honestly, not aspirationally.

1. **Time:** How many uninterrupted hours per day can you watch markets?
2. **Capital:** How much can you lose without changing your life?
3. **Temperament:** Do you prefer fast decisions or patient waiting?
4. **Skill:** Can you read structure, size a position and journal consistently?
5. **Cost:** Does your expected edge survive brokerage, STT, slippage and taxes?
6. **Risk capacity:** Can you survive a 20–30% drawdown without abandoning the plan?

If any answer is "I don't know", start with **delivery/swing** and paper trading.

chunks.title: 📚 Books — The Advanced Reading List > Reading method
chunks.text:
📚 Books — The Advanced Reading List > Reading method
Reading method

1. Read one chapter, write 5 bullet points.
2. Apply one idea to a chart/company.
3. Add one rule to your checklist.
4. Re-read the best 5 books yearly.

**Avoid:** get-rich-quick books, "sure-shot" systems, and anything that promises
returns without risk.

🔬 Research Notes — What This Course Is Built On > 1. Primary market history > BSE
BSE
- Founded **9 July 1875** as the Native Share & Stock Brokers' Association by
  Premchand Roychand; Asia's oldest exchange.
- Origins: 1850s informal trading under a banyan tree by five brokers.
- 1899: Dalal Street headquarters.
- 1957: first exchange recognised under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956.
- 1995: BOLT electronic trading.
- 2007: demutualised/corporatised.
- 2017: listed on NSE.

Source: Wikipedia — Bombay Stock Exchange (accessed Nov 2026); BSE corporate profile.
